source_record.Deficiency Description: Initial Comments - Not A Deficiency Citation
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1): This report is the result of an unannounced Federal Recertification Survey and State Re-licensure Survey completed on August 23, 2024 at Patient Care. It was determined the facility is not in substantial compliance with Federal requirements of 42 CFR Part 484, Subpart B Conditions of Participation for Home Health Agencies and State requirements of N.J.A.C. Title 8 Chapter 42 Home Health Agency Licensing Standards. Standard deficiencies were cited.

Encoding and transmitting OASIS
CFR(s): 484.45(a)
Standard: An HHA must encode and electronically transmit each completed OASIS assessment to the CMS system, regarding each beneficiary with respect to which information is required to be transmitted (as determined by the Secretary), within 30 days of completing the assessment of the beneficiary.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on review of facility documents and staff interview, it was determined the facility failed to electronically submit completed OASIS assessments to the CMS system within 30 days of completing the assessment of the beneficiary. 

Findings include:

On 8/22/24 at 11:09 AM, the OASIS report, "HHA [Home Health Agency] Error Summary by Agency Report" was electronically run in the presence of Staff (S) 4 (Executive Director) and was found to have 1,956 records with errors, 3330, "Record Submitted Late: The submission date is more than 30 days after M0090 (Date Assessment Completed) on this new record." 

On 8/22/24 at 11:15 AM, an interview with S4 (Executive Director) indicated that they [the facility] is aware and track every late upload from a quality standpoint.

On 8/23/24 at 11:09 AM, during an interview with S4 and S1 (Patient Care Manager), S4 stated there are quality reviewers (QR's) who monitor this and the information is found on the electronic dashboard. 

Facility Document titled, "Patient Care - W. [West] Orange, NJ Special Project," provided by S4 outlines the process the facility used to address the significant backlog of OASIS states, "...10/16/23[:] Clean Up Project initiated to address remaining backlog of OASIS assessments..." A line graph [graphical display of information that changes continuously over time], was attached to this document which includes the numerical percentage of "Late Locks" (late uploads) to the left monthly from April 2023-July 2024. Although this graph shows a fluctuating and overall decrease in trend, 8.17% late uploads were recorded in July 2024. S4 stated, "we are aware and take this very seriously."

N.J.A.C. 8.42-3.1(d)

Accessibility
CFR(s): 484.50(f)(1,2)
Standard: Accessibility.  Information must be provided to patients in plain language and in a manner that is accessible and timely to-

(1) Persons with disabilities, including accessible web sites and the provision of auxiliary aids and services at no cost to the individual in accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.

(2) Persons with limited English proficiency through the provision of language services at no cost to the individual, including oral interpretation and written translations.Standard: Accessibility  

Information must be provided to patients in plain language and in a manner that is accessible and timely to-

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation, staff interviews, medical record review, and review of facility policy and procedure, it was determined that the facility failed to provide language translation services to a non-English speaking patient according to facility policy in one of four medical records reviewed (Patient (P) 7).

Findings inlcude:

On 8/22/24 at 10:34 AM, P7’s initial Physical Therapy home visit was observed. During the evaluation, Staff (S) 10, Physical Therapist, communicated with P7 through his/her spouse. In the middle of the visit, at 11:00 AM, S10 asked P7’s spouse what language the patient speaks. S10 was informed that P7 spoke Russian.

On 8/22/24 at 11:25 AM, an interview was conducted with S10 after the home visit was completed. S10 reported that all staff have access to interpreter services on their tablets. S10 explained that he/she typically uses family members for translation if they are present during the treatment. According to S10, they usually only need the interpreter services on the tablet if the patient is alone.

On 8/23/24 at 11:30 AM, P7’s medical record was reviewed. The admission assessment was completed on 8/20/24 at 2:17 PM. P7’s response to “What is your preferred language?” was “Russian.” P7’s response to “Do you need or want an interpreter to communicate with a doctor or health care staff?” was “Yes.”

On 8/23/24 at 11:45 AM, S1, Patient Care Manager, reported that typically family is used to interpret for the patient. According to S1, patients are informed during the admission process that interpreters are available and the facility is usually made aware that an interpreter is needed during the referral process. S1 explained that staff would document use of an interpreter or offering of an interpreter in the narrative section of the clinician’s documentation.

On 8/23/24 at 12:20 PM, S1 and S4, Executive Director, explained that the question asked on admission, “Do you need or want an interpreter to communicate with a doctor or health care staff,” does not imply the patient wants to use interpreter services. S1 and S4 stated that a “yes” answer to this question means that the patient just wants someone to interpret for them, and this could be family.

S4 was unable to provide evidence in the medical record that P7 was offered interpreter services. The medical record lacked evidence that P7 was offered and/or declined the use of professional interpreter services as per facility policy.  

Facility Policy titled, “Limited English Proficiency Persons (LEP)” last reviewed on July 1, 2024, stated, “…Procedure: 1. On admission the patient/family/caregiver will be informed that interpreter services including American Sign Language (ASL) are available. If an individual is identified as a LEP person during the admission process, the agency will make formal arrangements with individuals or organizations to obtain the services of a qualified interpreter when needed….5. Family and friends may not be used to interpret or translate unless client/LEP person is made aware of the availability of interpreters at no charge, and then without coercion, chooses family or friends…When it is expressed by the patient that this service is not wanted (including remote interpreter services), the agency will oblige the patient’s request to allow a family member in order to meet patient’s Rights and Responsibilities in accordance with the agency official policies and procedures. Such an offer and the response will be documented in the patient’s medical record.”

N.J.A.C. 8:42-13.2(a)5

Infection Prevention
CFR(s): 484.70(a)
Standard: Infection Prevention.  

The HHA must follow accepted standards of practice, including the use of standard precautions, to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation, facility policy review and staff interviews, it was determined the facility failed to provide a sanitary environment by ensuring equipment that is used for more than one patient is disinfected between each patient use. 

On 8/21/24 at 1:42 PM, during a home visit with Patient (P) 2, Staff (S) 3 (Registered Nurse), was observed taking a tablet out of his/her bag and using it to document during the patient’s home visit. At 2:38 PM, at the conclusion of the visit, S3 provided the tablet to P2, and the patient used his/her finger to sign the tablet. S3 then carried the tablet out of the patient’s home. The tablet was not cleaned following contact with the patient. 

On 8/23/24 at 12:10 PM, S4 (Executive Director), confirmed “the tablet has to be wiped down with a low-level disinfectant after the patient signs.”

The facility policy titled, “Cleaning of Re-Usable Equipment” revised date 6/1/22, states, “…Policy: Equipment used for more than one patient is cleaned between each patient use. …Procedure 1. Non-critical items which will come in contact with intact patient skin will undergo a low-level disinfection between each patient use. …”

N.J.A.C. 8:42-12.3 (a)4

Findings include:

On 8/21/24 at 1:08 PM, Staff (S) 7, an Occupational Therapist (OT) was observed providing care for P4.

At 1:29 PM, S7 began taking P4’s vital signs with gloves on.

At 1:31 PM, S7 began entering the vital signs into his/her tablet without doffing gloves and performing hand hygiene.

At 1:37 PM, S7 began cleaning vital signs equipment (stethoscope, oximeter, blood pressure cuff and sphygmomanometer) with disinfectant wipes but failed to clean the tablet.

At 1:41 PM, P4 signed the tablet using his/her finger.

At 1:53 PM, the visit was completed and S7 exited P4’s home without cleaning the tablet. When questioned about the tablet, S7 stated that he/she should have cleaned the tablet before leaving P4’s home.

On 8/22/24 at 11:05 AM, an interview was conducted with S8, a Physical Therapist (PT). When questioned about tablets, he/she stated that the facility policy is to clean the tablet before leaving the patient’s house once patient care is completed.

Written notice for non-covered care
CFR(s): 484.50(c)(8)
Receive proper written notice, in advance of a specific service being furnished, if the HHA believes that the service may be non-covered care; or in advance of the HHA reducing or terminating on-going care. The HHA must also comply with the requirements of 42 CFR 405.1200 through 405.1204.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on medical record review and staff interview, it was determined the facility failed to ensure one out of five medical records reviewed (Patient (P) 17) received written notice of non-covered care, prior to discharge.

Findings include:

On 8/23/24, a review of P17’s medical record indicated he/she was discharged from homecare services on 10/31/23. Review of P17's medical record lacked evidence that he/she received a Notice of Medicare Non-Coverage (NOMNC); a notice that indicates when care is set to end from a home health agency. 

On 8/23/24 at 12:20 PM, Staff (S)4 (Executive Director) confirmed this finding.

N.J.A.C. 8.42-3.1(d)

Required items in clinical record
CFR(s): 484.110(a)(1)
The patient's current comprehensive assessment, including all of the assessments from the most recent home health admission, clinical notes, plans of care, and physician or allowed practitioner orders;

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on medical record review, staff interviews, and review of facility policy and procedure, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that patient’s medical records are completed within 24 hours, as per facility policy in eight out of 12 medical records reviewed (Patient (P) 1, P5, P8, P9, P13, P14, P16, and P17).

Findings include:

Patient (P) 1’s medical record was reviewed on 8/22/24 at 12:30 PM, the following was revealed:                                                                                                                                                                                                                    P1 was admitted to home care services on 7/27/24 for Physical Therapy (PT) for right hip pain.  
On 8/2/24, P1 was seen in-home by PT at 9:28 AM. The visit note was completed on 8/4/24 at 6:46 PM.
On 8/6/24, P1 was seen in-home by PT at 12:00 PM. The visit note was completed on 8/8/24 at 11:04 AM.
On 8/8/24, P1 was seen in-home by PT at 11:05 AM. The visit note was completed on 8/11/24 at 7:11 PM.
On 8/14/24, P1 was seen in home by PT at 2:14 PM. The visit note was completed on 8/18/24 at 9:14 AM.

P5’s medical record was reviewed on 8/22/24 at 12:30 PM, the following was revealed:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   On 7/2/24, P5 was seen in-home for a Skilled Nurse (SN) visit at 12:58 PM. The visit note was completed on 7/12/24 at 7:15 AM.

source_record.Deficiency Description: Initial Comments - Not A Deficiency Citation
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
This was a Federal Recertification Survey and a Federal COVID-19 Focused Infection Control Survey conducted on October 6, October 7, and October 8, 2021. Patient Care is not in compliance with 42 CFR Part 484, Subpart B requirements, for Home Health Agencies.

As a result of this survey, Standard level deficiencies were cited.

Infection Prevention
CFR(s): 484.70(a)
Standard: Infection Prevention.  

The HHA must follow accepted standards of practice, including the use of standard precautions, to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation in three (3) of five (5) home visits, staff interview, and review of facility documents, it was determined the facility failed to ensure infection prevention measures are implemented to prevent the spread of infections and communicable diseases. 

Reference: Facility policy titled "Standard Precautions" states, "...remove gloves promptly after use, before touching non contaminated items and environmental surfaces, and perform hand hygiene immediately after completing patient care activities to avoid transfer of microorganisms to other patients or environments. … ."

1. On 10/6/21 at 2:14 PM, a home visit was conducted and the following was observed: 

a. Patient #1's caregiver held the facility's tablet and signed for the service that was rendered on that day. Staff #10 failed to decontaminate the tablet after the caregiver had it in his/her possession.

2. On 10/7/21 at 1:05 PM, a home visit was conducted and the following was observed: 

a. Staff #12 donned gloves and obtained Patient #1's vital signs. After completing Patient #1's vital signs, Staff #12 sanitized his/her gloves then entered his/her bag. 

(i)  At 1:15 PM, Staff #12 sanitized his/her gloves after touching an inanimate object.

3. Staff #1 confirmed that the above findings were not in accordance with facility policy.

N.J.A.C 8:42-12.3(a)(4) 

Findings include:

 

Reference: Facility Policy titled, “Hand Hygiene” states, “Purpose: To help prevent the spread of microorganisms and infection by cross-contamination and to provide guidelines. Policy: Staff are required to perform hand hygiene prior to, at specified time points during, and following patient contact. Hand hygiene will be performed using soap and water or an alcohol-based hand sanitizer. … .”

 

1. On 10/7/21 at 1:45 PM, a Home Visit for Patient #5 was conducted, and the following was observed:

a. At the conclusion of the Home Visit, Staff #5 handed Patient #5 the electronic tablet and asked the patient to sign for receipt of the visit. After signing, the patient handed the tablet back to Staff #5. The staff donned gloves, cleaned the tablet with a cleansing wipe, and then doffed his/her gloves. Staff #5 then exited the home.  Staff #5 did not perform hand hygiene after cleaning the tablet the patient had touched and prior to exiting the home.  

 

2. The above was confirmed by Staff #5 at the end of the visit.  

N.J.A.C 8:42-12.3(a)(4)

Infection control
CFR(s): 484.70(b)(1)(2)
Standard: Control.  

The HHA must maintain a coordinated agency-wide program for the surveillance, identification, prevention, control, and investigation of infectious and communicable diseases that is an integral part of the HHA's quality assessment and performance improvement (QAPI) program. The infection control program must include:



(1) A method for identifying infectious and communicable disease problems; and



(2) A plan for the appropriate actions that are expected to result in improvement and disease prevention.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation in two (2) of five (5) home visits, staff interviews, and review of facility documents, it was determined the facility failed to implement their protocol for identifying, controlling, and/or preventing infections and communicable disease by ensuring that COVID-19 screening is completed prior to staff entering the patient’s residence.

Findings include:

 

Reference: Facility Policy titled, “Exposure to Coronavirus-(COVID-19): Disease Response and Management Policy #9.1.014”, states, “Purpose: The purpose of this policy is to follow the recommendations of the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) … by providing guidance on effective and legally compliant responses to reports of potential COVID-19 exposure. … . Screening and Assessment of Patients and Patient Care settings:  … . 2. Patients should be assessed prior to each visit for exposure associated with risk of COVID-19 infections (e.g., travel to geographically affected areas, close contact with confirmed cases, or persons under suspicion for Covid-19, or contact with family members/friends who have traveled to geographically affected areas.) … . 4. Patients who report having symptoms and meet the criteria of the clinical features for Covid-19 should be asked to wear a surgical mask, and if possible, should be separated them at six (6) feet from other persons. face shield) should also be donned. 5. If a patient meets the criteria to be classified as a suspected or confirmed COVID-19 patient, employees must notify their immediate supervisor and the attending Physician. … . 6.Employees involved in the care of confirmed or suspected COVID-19 patients must use standard precautions, contact precautions, and airborne precautions, and droplet precautions. N95 Face masks as well as the use of eye protection (goggles or face shield) must be donned. Surgical face masks are not to be used for visits on confirmed or suspected Covid-19 patients. … .” 

 

1. On 10/7/21 at 10:10 AM, a home visit for Patient # 3 was conducted and the following was observed:  

a. Staff #11 entered the Patient’s home and while making introductions and setting up his/her workspace, he/she verbally inquired if the patient was experiencing any symptoms indicative of Covid-19 or had any exposure to a person with known or suspected Covid-19.   

b. At the conclusion of the home visit, Staff #11 was interviewed about the agencies Patient Screening protocols/policies, and the following was indicated: 

(i)  Staff #11 stated that he/she conducts the Covid-19 screening of patients upon entering the home for the visit. 

2. On 10/7/21 at 11:55 AM, Staff #1 was interviewed about the agency Patient Screening protocols/policies, and the following was indicated: 

a. Staff #11 stated that the staff will either call their patients the night before their visit to conduct a Covid-19 Screening or the screening is done within their visit once the home is entered.  Staff are required to wear standard PPE (Personal Protective Equipment) for all visits which consist of a surgical mask and eye protection.  If caring for a Covid-19 positive patient, the staff would be required to wear full PPE such as an N95 mask, goggles or face shield, gloves, and gown. 

 

3. On 10/7/21 at 1:45 PM, a home visit for Patient #5 was conducted, and the following was observed:

a.  Staff #17 entered the patient’s home and proceeded to inquire if the patient had any physical symptoms that would be consistent with Covid-19.  In addition, he/she inquired to the patient about his/her contact with others and if there was a potential exposure the patient may have had to Covid-19.  

 

(i)  Staff #17 was interviewed regarding the time frame for performing a Covid-19 symptom and exposure assessment.  He/she stated that he/she performs this screening after he/she enters the home.  

 

4. Upon review of the above referenced agency policy and procedure, patients should be assessed prior to each visit.  

 

5. On 10/8/21, the above findings were reviewed with and confirmed by Staff #1.

N.J.A.C 8:42-12.2(5)

source_record.Deficiency Description: Promptly Alert Relevant Physician Of Changes
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Promptly alert relevant physician of changes
CFR(s): 484.60(c)(1)
The HHA must promptly alert the relevant physician(s) or allowed practitioner(s) to any changes in the patient's condition or needs that suggest that outcomes are not being achieved and/or that the plan of care should be altered.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on medical record review and staff interview, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that the physician is informed of the recommendation for additional Occupational Therapy visits.

Findings include:

1. On 10/8/21, upon review of Medical Record #2, the following was noted:

2. Patient #2 was evaluated by an Occupational Therapist on 7/8/21. The Visit Note Report states, "...Therapy Assessment/Plan...Recommend two additional occupational therapy visits at this time to review home exercise program and range of motion. ..." 

3. There was no evidence that the physician was made aware of the recommendation. There was no further documentation or new orders regarding the recommendation. 

4. The above finding was confirmed by Staff #9.

Patients receive education and training
CFR(s): 484.60(d)(5)
Ensure that each patient, and his or her caregiver(s) where applicable, receive ongoing education and training provided by the HHA, as appropriate, regarding the care and services identified in the plan of care.  The HHA must provide training, as necessary, to ensure a timely discharge.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on review of 1 (one) of 5 (five) medical records (#1), staff interview and document review, it was determined that the facility failed to provide individualized patient specific education.

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy titled, "Patient Education" states, "...PROCEDURE: ...3. The patient and caregiver receive ongoing information specific to the identified needs, ..." 

1. Review of Medical Record #1 on 10/8/21 revealed the following:

a. Patient #1 was an 83 year old female.

b. The Visit Note Report dated 10/1/2021, under the section identified as "Patient Goals," states, "Prevent Falls." In the section identified as "Narrative" it states,  "...Stop smoking ...Change from oral contraceptives to another form of birth control. Safety measures and fall prevention reinforced, ..." 

(i) Staff #9 stated that the above was considered patient education.

c. There was no evidence in the medical record that Patient #1 had a history of smoking. 

d. There was no evidence that Patient #1 was prescribed oral contraceptives. 

2. Staff #9 confirmed that the patient education pertaining to smoking and oral contraceptives were not applicable to Patient #1.

source_record.Deficiency Description: Initial Comments - Not A Deficiency Citation
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
A Federal Recertification survey was conducted on October 15-17, 2018, that resulted in Standard level deficiencies.

Eleven (11) Medical Records were reviewed.

Five (5) Home visits were conducted.

Plan of care
CFR(s): 484.60(a)(1)
Each patient must receive the home health services that are written in an individualized plan of care that identifies patient-specific measurable outcomes and goals, and which is established, periodically reviewed, and signed by a doctor of medicine, osteopathy, or podiatry acting within the scope of his or her state license, certification, or registration. If a physician refers a patient under a plan of care that cannot be completed until after an evaluation visit, the physician is consulted to approve additions or modifications to the original plan.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on staff interview and document review, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that patient visits are provided in accordance with the plan of care. 

Findings include:

1. Medical Record #11 - The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care form, Start of Care dated 9/8/18, for the Certification Period 9/8/18 to 11/6/18 stated, "Frequency /Duration of Visits: SN [skilled nursing] 1WK1 [one visit during the first week], 2WK3 [two visits per week for three weeks], 1WK3 [one visit per week for three weeks]." 

a. The nursing Visit Note Report lacked evidence of a 2nd visit made during the week of 9/9/18.

2. Medical Record #7- The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care form, Start of Care dated 8/12/18, for the Certification Period 8/12/18 to 10/18/18 stated, "Frequency/Duration of Visits: HHA [home health aide] effective 8/19/2018 2WK3 [two visits per week for three weeks], 1 WK1 [one visit for one week]."

a. Review of the home health aide visits revealed that no aide visit was performed during the week of 9/9/18. 

3. The above was confirmed by Staff #4.

Infection Prevention
CFR(s): 484.70(a)
Standard: Infection Prevention.  

The HHA must follow accepted standards of practice, including the use of standard precautions, to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
A. Based on observation, staff interview and review of facility documents, it was determined that the facility failed to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases in accordance with nationally recognized guidelines. 

Findings includes:

Reference: Guideline for Hand Hygiene in Health Care Settings: Recommendation of the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee[HICPAC] and the HICPAC/SHEA/APIC/IDSA Hand Hygiene Task Force, published in the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report at MMWR 2002; 51 (No. RR-16) page 32 states, "Recommendations:

1. Indications for Handwashing and Hand antisepsis ...

C. Decontaminate hands before having direct contact with patients...

F. Decontaminate hands after contact with a patient's intact skin ...

G. Decontaminate hands after contact with...a patient's nonintact skin ...

I. Decontaminate hands after contact with inanimate objects...in the immediate vicinity of the patient.

J. Decontaminate hands after removing gloves..."

1. On 10/15/18, during a home visit for Patient #1, Staff #8 was observed assisting the patient with ADLs (Activities of Daily Living).

a. While the patient was in the shower, Staff #8 used his/her gloved hands to pick up the bath mat from the hallway floor and placed it on the bathroom floor. 

b. With the same gloves, Staff #8 then proceeded to apply lotion to the patient's back and assisted with dressing the patient. 

2. Staff #8 failed to doff gloves and perform hand hygiene after contact with the bath mat, and before having direct contact with the patient. 

3. The above findings were confirmed with Staff #1. 

B. Based on observation, staff interview and review of facility documents, it was determined that the facility failed to develop a written policy and procedure for handling, storage, cleaning and disinfecting of electronic devices.

Findings include:

Reference: CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities, 2008 states, "Ensure that, at a minimum, noncritical patient-care devices are disinfected when visibly soiled and on a regular basis (such as after use on each patient ...)". 

1. On 10/15/18, Staff #8 was observed documenting on an electronic tablet. Staff #8 then asked Patient #1 to sign on the electronic tablet using his/her index finger. 

a. Staff #8 failed to clean and disinfect the electronic device before and after patient use. 

2. On interview, Staff #3 stated that the cleaning and disinfecting of electronic devices fall under the policy for equipment cleaning.

3. Upon review of the "Staff Equipment" policy and procedure, it was revealed that the policy for cleaning "Staff Equipment" only contains procedures for cleaning and disinfecting blood pressure cuffs, stethoscopes and thermometers. 

4. The above findings were confirmed with Staff #2.

Discharge plans communication
CFR(s): 484.60(c)(3)(ii)
(ii) Any revisions related to plans for the patient's discharge must be communicated to the patient, representative, caregiver, all physicians issuing orders for the HHA plan of care, and the patient's primary care practitioner or other health care professional who will be responsible for providing care and services to the patient after discharge from the HHA  (if any).

This Element is not met as evidenced by:

Based on document review and staff interview, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that revision to discharge plans are discussed with the patient.

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy "Plan of Care" states, "Procedure for the Start of Care ... 10. Initially and as changes occur in the care, whether by the agency or the physician or at the request of the patient, there is evidence in the clinical record that the patient was consulted and consented to the planned services and care."

1. Medical Record #11- The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care Start of Care dated 9/8/18, for the Certification Period 9/8/18 to 11/6/18 stated, "Frequency /Duration of Visits: SN [skilled nursing] 1WK1 [one visit during the first week], 2WK3 [two visits per week for three weeks], 1WK3 [one visit per week for three weeks]." 

a. Nursing services began on 9/8/18. The patient was discharged from nursing services on 9/25/18. 

b. There was no evidence of an ongoing dialogue with the patient regarding discharge from service until the visit of 9/25/18.

c. The above was confirmed by Staff #4.

Patients receive education and training
CFR(s): 484.60(d)(5)
Ensure that each patient, and his or her caregiver(s) where applicable, receive ongoing education and training provided by the HHA, as appropriate, regarding the care and services identified in the plan of care.  The HHA must provide training, as necessary, to ensure a timely discharge.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:

Based on document review and staff interview, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that the patient is provided education as identified in the plan of care.

Findings include:

1. Medical Record #6 -The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care Start of Care dated 7/12/18, for the Certification Period 7/12/18 to 9/9/18 stated, " ... Provide teaching on sign/symptoms of CHF [congestive heart failure], hospitalization risk reduction, ... modification of risk factors and self-management principles related to the CHF disease process."

a. The Visit Notes Report from 7/15/18 until 9/5/18, a total of 9 visits, lacked evidence of any teaching related to CHF, hospitalization risk reduction, modification of risk factors and self-management principle related to the disease.

2. Medical Record #9 - The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care dated 8/29/18, for the Certification Period 8/29/18 to 10/27/18 stated, "... provide skilled teaching of management of respiratory disease in the home setting, including diet, medication therapy and activities permitted/restrictions."

a. The Visit Notes Report from 8/29/18 until 10/5/18, a total of 6 visits, lacked evidence of any teaching related to diet, medication therapy and activities permitted/restrictions. 

3. The above findings were confirmed with Staff #4.

Interdisciplinary assessment of the patient
CFR(s): 484.75(b)(1)
Ongoing interdisciplinary assessment of the patient;

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on medical record review and staff interview, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure sharing of information occurred between nursing staff and therapy.

Findings include:

1. Medical Record #7 - The patient began home health services on 8/12/18. A Visit Note Report indicated a home visit made by a LPN [licensed practical nurse] on 9/5/18. In the Narrative section of the note, it was indicated that the patient was unable to get up from the bedside commode back to the chair and that the fire department was called to help. The note also indicated that a call was placed to the physician regarding a cough with greenish sputum, and that an appointment was made.

2. There was no evidence that the nursing case manager or physical therapist was notified of the above events. The patient was discharged from physical therapy services on 9/7/18.

3. The above was confirmed by Staff #4.

source_record.Deficiency Description: Provide Services In The Plan Of Care
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Provide services in the plan of care
CFR(s): 484.75(b)(3)
Providing services that are ordered by the physician as indicated in the plan of care;

This Element is not met as evidenced by:

Based on document review and staff interview, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that wound care orders are performed and that the wound care policy was implemented.

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy "Wound Management" states, "... Procedure to Measure a Wound 

Wound are measured upon admission, upon development, and at the first visit after any interruption in service, and then after baseline, on a weekly basis to assess healing progress."

1. Medical Record #8 - The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care Start of Care dated 8/20/18, for the Certification Period 8/20/18 to 10/18/18 indicated skilled nursing visit effective 8/23/18 for wound management. 

a. On 8/23/18, a wound to the lateral left foot was assessed, as per policy.

b. The next time the wound was measured was on 9/7/18 and refused by the patient on 9/17/18.

c. Wound measurements were not taken during the week of 8/26/18 and during the week of 9/9/18.

2. Medical Record #10 - The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care Start of Care dated 1/13/18, for the Certification Period 9/10/18 to 11/8/18 "Orders of Discipline and Treatments: ... Skilled Nurse to perform/teach daily wound care to cranial head mass. Cleanse daily with NSS [normal sterile saline], apply antifungal cream, cover with optilock pad, secure with tape."

a. Review of the medication list revealed that Bacitracin Topical was ordered for the cranial mass.

b. Review of the nursing Visit Notes report dated 9/18 and 9/26/18 revealed that an antifungal cream was applied.

c. The wound care order was not clarified until 10/3/18.

3. The above was confirmed with Staff #4.

Communication with physicians
CFR(s): 484.75(b)(7)
Communication with all physicians involved in the plan of care and other health care practitioners (as appropriate) related to the current plan of care;

This Element is not met as evidenced by:

Based on document review, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that nursing staff communicated with the physician a change in the plan of care.

Findings include:

1. Medical Record #7 - The nursing Visit Note Report dated 8/12/18 for the Home Health Certification and Plan of Care Start of Care for the Certification Period 8/12/18 to 10/10/18 indicated that the patient refused telehealth monitor. One of the interventions provided stated, "3 HRH Program ... Explained that the telehealth monitor will be installed in the home on visit number 2, the next day."

a. Visit #2 was done on 8/15/18. There was no evidence that a Telehealth monitor was installed.

b. Visit #3 was done on 8/17/18. One of the interventions provided, "Will assess the use of Telehealth and reinforce the importance for the daily use of Telehealth when installed."

c. Visit #5 was done on 8/24/18. One of the interventions provided, "... Completed Telehealth enrollment form."

d. On 9/19/18 discharge visit, there was no evidence that the patient was placed on Telehealth. There was no documentation to indicate that the physician was made aware.

e. The above was confirmed with Staff #4.

Onsite supervisory visit every 14 days
CFR(s): 484.80(h)(1)(i)
If home health aide services are provided to a patient who is receiving skilled nursing, physical or occupational therapy, or speech-language pathology services, a registered nurse or other appropriate skilled professional who is familiar with the patient, the patient's plan of care, and the written patient care instructions described in §484.80(g), must make an onsite visit to the patient's home no less frequently than every 14 days. The home health aide does not have to be present during this visit.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on medical record review, staff interview and review of facility documents, it was determined that the registered nurse failed to make home health aide supervisory visits every two weeks. 

Findings include: 

Reference: Facility policy titled "Supervision" states, "... e. For patients with a skill, the registered nurse provides on-site HHA supervision every 14 days... The supervisory visit documentation is filed in the patient's medical record."

1. Review of Medical Record #9 revealed the following:

a. A Skilled Nursing and Home Health Aid Supervisory Visit was scheduled on 9/8/18. 

b. Medical Record #9 indicated that Supervisory Functions were not performed. 

c. The next Supervisory Visit was performed on 9/19/18. 

2. The registered nurse failed to make home health aide supervisory visits every two weeks.

3. The above finding was confirmed with Staff #4.

Required items in clinical record
CFR(s): 484.110(a)(1)
The patient's current comprehensive assessment, including all of the assessments from the most recent home health admission, clinical notes, plans of care, and physician orders;

This Element is not met as evidenced by:

Based on document review and staff interview, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that an accurate assessment of the patient is performed and documented.

Findings include:

1. Medical Record #7 - The patient began receiving home health services from 8/12/18 and was discharged on 9/19/18. 

a. Physical therapy services were provided. Review of the Visit Note Report (a total of 8 visits) revealed that the patient had pitting edema of the lower right and lower left ranging from 1+ to 2+.

b. Nursing services were provided. Review of the Visit Note Report (a total of 12 visit) lacked evidence of edema of the lower extremities. In some instances, the nursing visits and physical therapy visits were performed on the same day and close in time of one another.

c. Documentation of the cardiovascular system was inconsistent between the disciplines. 

d. The above was confirmed by Staff #4.

source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Plan of care
CFR(s): 484.60(a)(1)
Each patient must receive the home health services that are written in an individualized plan of care that identifies patient-specific measurable outcomes and goals, and which is established, periodically reviewed, and signed by a doctor of medicine, osteopathy, or podiatry acting within the scope of his or her state license, certification, or registration. If a physician refers a patient under a plan of care that cannot be completed until after an evaluation visit, the physician is consulted to approve additions or modifications to the original plan.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
A. Based on medical record review, review of facility policy and procedure, and staff interviews, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that patient visits are provided in accordance with the plan of care. 

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy, Field Clinician's Missed Visit Process, states, "...1. In the event of a scheduled visit is being missed, please select the appropriate reason. 2. If missed visit is early in the Medicare week, the case manager will reassign the case within the week. 3. Communicate the missed visit to the physician. 4. Document reason in Missed Visit Notification note. 5. it is the clinician's responsibility to ensure that the next scheduled visit is reassigned for that week in order to be compliant with the visit frequencies on the Plan of Care. 6. Obtain verbal orders as appropriate from the physician. 7. Adjust the calendar to match the visit frequency."

1. Upon review of Medical Record #6, the following was noted:

a. The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care form, Start of Care dated 12/20/18, for the Certification Period 12/20/18 to 2/17/19 stated, "Frequency / Duration of Visits: SN [skilled nursing] 1WK1 [one visit during the first week], 3WK2 [three visits per week for two weeks], 2WK4 [two visits per week for four weeks], 1WK1 [one visit per week for one week] ... HHA [home health aide] effective 12/23/18 3WK6 [three visits per week for six weeks]." 

i. One (1) skilled nursing visit was missed the week of 12/23/18.

ii. Two (2) home health aide visits were missed the week of 12/23/18.

iii. One (1) home health aide visit was missed the week of 12/30/18.

iv. One (1) skilled nursing visit was missed the week of 1/6/19.

v. There was no documented evidence the physician was notified that the above visits were missed. 

2. Upon review of the Medical Record #8, the following was noted:

a. The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care From, Start of Care dated 11/8/18, for the Certification Period 11/8/18 to 1/6/19 stated, "Frequency/Duration of Visits: SN 2WK2 [2 visits per week for 2 weeks], 3WK7 [3 visits per week for 7 weeks]".

i. There was a SN visit missed the week of 12/16/18. 

ii. There was no documented evidence the physician was notified that the above visit was missed.

3. Upon review of Medical Record #10, the following was noted:

a. The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care form, Start of Care dated 10/31/18, for the Certification Period 10/31/18 to 12/29/18 stated, "Frequency/Duration of Visits: ...OT (Occupational Therapy) 1WK1 [1 time per week for 1 week]."

i. A physician order, dated 11/4/18, stated "Occupational Therapy Patient missed OT visit week of 10/29/18. Continue Skilled OT Services for OT Evaluation and Treatment 11/5/18."

b. There was an OT missed visit on 11/5/18.

i. There was no documented evidence the physician was notified that the above visit was missed. 

c. Patient #10 was not evaluated by the OT service during the Certification Period of 10/31/18 to 12/29/18.

5. The above findings were confirmed with Staff #4 and Staff #13.

B. Based on medical record review, review of facility policy and procedure, and staff interviews, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that patients' wounds are measured in accordance with facility policy. 

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy, Wound Measurement, Dressing Change and Photography Policy, states, "...Measure wound on admission, resumption of care or first visit of the week (preferred) and prn [as needed], any change in wound status/condition, and document. ..." 

1. Upon review of Medical Record #7, the following was noted:

a. The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care form, Start of Care dated 12/1/18, for the Certification Period 12/1/18 to 1/29/2019 stated, "Frequency /Duration of Visits: SN [skilled nursing] 1WK5 [one visit per week for five weeks] ..."

b. The patient had an admission assessment on 12/1/18. It was documented in the assessment that the patient had a pressure ulcer of the sacral region. The wound was measured and assessed.

c. One skilled nurse visit was made during the week of 12/16/18. The wound was not measured or assessed. 

2. Upon review of Medical Record #10, the following was noted:

a. The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care form, Start of Care dated 10/31/18, for the Certification Period 10/31/18 to 12/29/18 stated, "Frequency/Duration of Visits: SN 2WK1 [2 visits per week for 1 week], 3WK1 [3 visits per week for 1 week], 2WK2 [2 visits per week for 2 weeks], 1WK2 [1 visit per week for 2 weeks]...".

b. The patient had an admission assessment on 10/31/18. It was documented in the assessment that the patient had a pressure ulcer of the left hip and a pressure ulcer to the sacral region. The wounds were measured and assessed.

c. A SN visit was made on 11/7/18. The wound was measured and assessed. 

d. The next SN visit was made on 11/24/18. The wound was not measured or assessed.

ii. Upon interview, Staff #5 stated that wounds should be measured at least once per week.

e. The wounds were not measured for twenty-two (22) days.

i. Upon interview, Staff #5 stated that a measurement should have been taken on 11/24/18. 

3. The above findings were confirmed with Staff #1, Staff #4, and Staff #5.

source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
EP Training Program
CFR(s): 484.102(d)(1)
§403.748(d)(1), §416.54(d)(1), §418.113(d)(1), §441.184(d)(1), §460.84(d)(1), §482.15(d)(1), §483.73(d)(1), §483.475(d)(1), §484.102(d)(1), §485.68(d)(1),  §485.542(d)(1), §485.625(d)(1), §485.727(d)(1), §485.920(d)(1), §486.360(d)(1), §491.12(d)(1).



*[For RNCHIs at §403.748, ASCs at §416.54, Hospitals at §482.15, ICF/IIDs at §483.475, HHAs at §484.102, REHs at §485.542, "Organizations" under §485.727, OPOs at §486.360, RHC/FQHCs at §491.12:]

 (1) Training program. The [facility] must do all of the following:

(i) Initial training in emergency preparedness policies and procedures to all new and existing staff, individuals providing services under arrangement, and volunteers, consistent with their expected roles.

(ii) Provide emergency preparedness training at least every 2 years.

(iii) Maintain documentation of all emergency preparedness training.

(iv) Demonstrate staff knowledge of emergency procedures.

(v) If the emergency preparedness policies and procedures are significantly updated, the [facility] must conduct training on the updated policies and procedures. 



*[For Hospices at §418.113(d):] (1) Training. The hospice must do all of the following:

(i) Initial training in emergency preparedness policies and procedures to all new and existing hospice employees, and individuals providing services under arrangement, consistent with their expected roles. 

(ii) Demonstrate staff knowledge of emergency procedures.

(iii) Provide emergency preparedness training at least every 2 years.

(iv) Periodically review and rehearse its emergency preparedness plan with hospice employees (including nonemployee staff), with special emphasis placed on carrying out the procedures necessary to protect patients and others.

(v) Maintain documentation of all emergency preparedness training.

(vi) If the emergency preparedness policies and procedures are significantly updated, the hospice must conduct training on the updated policies and

procedures.



*[For PRTFs at §441.184(d):] (1) Training program. The PRTF must do all of the following:

(i) Initial training in emergency preparedness policies and procedures to all new and existing staff, individuals providing services under arrangement, and volunteers, consistent with their expected roles.

(ii) After initial training, provide emergency preparedness training every 2 years.

(iii) Demonstrate staff knowledge of emergency procedures.

(iv) Maintain documentation of all emergency preparedness training.

(v) If the emergency preparedness policies and procedures are significantly updated, the PRTF must conduct training on the updated policies and procedures.   



*[For PACE at §460.84(d):] (1) The PACE organization must do all of the following:

(i) Initial training in emergency preparedness policies and procedures to all new and existing staff, individuals providing on-site services under arrangement, contractors, participants, and volunteers, consistent with their expected roles.

(ii) Provide emergency preparedness training at least every 2 years.

(iii) Demonstrate staff knowledge of emergency procedures, including informing participants of what to do, where to go, and whom to contact in case of an emergency.

(iv) Maintain documentation of all training.

(v)  If the emergency preparedness policies and procedures are significantly updated, the PACE must conduct training on the updated policies and procedures.



*[For LTC Facilities at §483.73(d):] (1) Training Program. The LTC facility must do all of the following:

(i) Initial training in emergency preparedness policies and procedures to all new and existing staff, individuals providing services under arrangement, and volunteers, consistent with their expected role.

(ii) Provide emergency preparedness training at least annually.

(iii) Maintain documentation of all emergency preparedness training.

(iv) Demonstrate staff knowledge of emergency procedures.



*[For CORFs at §485.68(d):](1) Training. The CORF must do all of the following:

(i) Provide initial training in emergency preparedness policies and procedures to all new and existing staff, individuals providing services under arrangement, and volunteers, consistent with their expected roles. 

(ii) Provide emergency preparedness training at least every 2 years.

(iii) Maintain documentation of the training.

(iv) Demonstrate staff knowledge of emergency procedures. All new personnel must be oriented and assigned specific responsibilities regarding the CORF's emergency plan within 2 weeks of their first workday. The training program must include instruction in the location and use of alarm systems and signals and firefighting equipment.

(v)   If the emergency preparedness policies and procedures are significantly updated, the CORF must conduct training on the updated policies and procedures.   



*[For CAHs at §485.625(d):] (1) Training program. The CAH must do all of the following:

(i) Initial training in emergency preparedness policies and procedures, including prompt reporting and extinguishing of fires, protection, and where necessary, evacuation of patients, personnel, and guests, fire prevention, and cooperation with firefighting and disaster authorities, to all new and existing staff, individuals providing services under arrangement, and volunteers, consistent with their expected roles.

(ii) Provide emergency preparedness training at least every 2 years.

(iii) Maintain documentation of the training.

(iv) Demonstrate staff knowledge of emergency procedures. 

(v)   If the emergency preparedness policies and procedures are significantly updated, the CAH must conduct training on the updated policies and procedures.   



*[For CMHCs at §485.920(d):] (1) Training.  The CMHC must provide initial training in emergency preparedness policies and procedures to all new and existing staff, individuals providing services under arrangement, and volunteers, consistent with their expected roles, and maintain documentation of the training.  The CMHC must demonstrate staff knowledge of emergency procedures.  Thereafter, the CMHC must provide emergency preparedness training at least every 2 years.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on personnel record review, review of facility documents, and staff interview, it was determined the facility failed to ensure staff received emergency preparedness training annually in accordance with facility policy for four of five personnel files reviewed (Staff (S) 1, S2, S9, and S11). 

 

 

Findings include:

Facility policy titled, “Emergency or Disaster Preparedness” dated 12/09/19, stated, “…Procedure…18. There will be initial in-servicing [sic] for all new employees and annual training on our Disaster Policy and Plan for all direct staff and those providing service under contract. Staff knowledge will be demonstrated through competency testing…”

Facility document titled, “[Facility Name] All Hazard Emergency Preparedness Plan” dated 01/26/26, stated, “…Planning: Administration:…4. All staff will receive emergency preparedness training appropriate for their position at orientation and then on a yearly basis. Staff will understand their roles and response protocols…”

On 06/03/26, the personnel files for S1, S2, S9, and S11 were reviewed and lacked evidence of annual Emergency Preparedness training. 

On 06/03/26 at 12:02 PM, an interview was conducted with S1. S1 explained he/she felt that participation in the mock drill would cover a staff member’s annual education. S1 reported all staff receive an email with information about the mock drill and emergency preparedness prior to the facility’s mock drills. S1 was unable to provide a copy of the email sent to the staff or evidence of staff receipt of this education. S1 confirmed that only staff working on the day of the mock drill participate in this training.

source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Infection Prevention
CFR(s): 484.70(a)
Standard: Infection Prevention.  

The HHA must follow accepted standards of practice, including the use of standard precautions, to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation, staff interview, and review of facility policy and procedure, it was determined the facility failed to ensure: 1. staff perform hand hygiene in accordance with facility policy, and 2. disinfect reusable patient care equipment and electronic medical devices in accordance with facility policy and/or instructions for use (IFU) of cleaning supplies, in one of seven home visits conducted (Patient (P)2).

 

Findings include:

1. Facility policy titled, “Hand Hygiene," dated 10/07/13, stated, “… Procedure: 1. Hand-hygiene technique: When decontaminating hands with an alcohol-based hand rub, apply product to palm of one hand and rub hands together, covering all surfaces of hands and fingers, until hands are dry…”

On 06/01/26 at 1:00 PM, Staff (S)9 was observed providing care for P2 during a home visit.

At 1:20 PM, after assisting P2 transfer from the toilet to a rollator (wheeled walker), S9 applied hand sanitizer. S9 rubbed his/her hands together and then blew on his/her hands. S9 stated, “Have to make sure they are dry.” S9 then contacted P2 with his/her hands and began therapy exercises.

At 1:42 PM, an interview was conducted with S9. When asked about the process for hand hygiene, S9 stated, he/she applies the hand sanitizer and waits for his/her hands to dry. S9 stated, if they are not completely dry, he/she might blow on them. S9 stated, he/she has never spit on his/her hands while blowing on them and would reapply hand sanitizer if he/she felt spit on his/her hands. 

On 06/03/26 at 1:00 PM, an interview was conducted with S1. When asked about the process for drying hands after applying hand sanitizer, S1 stated, hands should be rubbed together until dry. S9 stated, staff should not blow on their hands to speed the drying process.

2. Facility policy titled, “Bag Technique and Equipment”, stated, “…VIII. Management of Electronic Medical Records Devices in the Home: … B. Wipe down Electronic Medical Record devices, i.e. smart phones, tablets, etc. with agency-approved disinfectant wipes, such as alcohol wipes, after completing each patient visit… Allow to dry.”

Disinfecting wipes labeled, “Sani-Cloth Germicidal Disposable Wipes,” stated, “Directions For Use: … TO DISINFECT AND DEODORIZE HARD, NONPOROUS SURFACES: … Unfold wipe and thoroughly wet surface. Allow surface to remain visibly wet for one (1) minute. Let air dry… FOR USE ON HARD, NONPOROUS SURFACES ONLY.”       

On 06/01/26 at 1:00 PM, S9 was observed providing care for P2 during a home visit.

At 1:03 PM, S9 was observed taking P2’s blood pressure using an automatic wrist blood pressure monitor. The material on the cuff of the monitor was a light gray, soft, porous fabric with visible light brown stains on the fabric.

At 1:27 PM, S9 used a Sani-Cloth wipe to clean the wrist blood pressure monitor and cuff.

At 1:29 PM, P2 used his/her finger to sign S9’s tablet.

At 1:30 PM, S9 used a Sani-Cloth wipe to clean the tablet. After cleaning the tablet, S9 placed it in his/her bag immediately without allowing one-minute dry time.

At 1:42 PM, an interview was conducted with S9. When asked about the wrist blood pressure monitor, S9 stated, he/she had purchased the monitor and it was not supplied by the facility. When asked about cleaning of equipment, S9 stated he/she uses Sani-Cloth wipes supplied by the agency which have a dry time of one minute.

On 06/03/26 at 1:00 PM, an interview was conducted with S1. When asked about cleaning of vital sign equipment, S9 stated, staff using their own blood pressure monitor and cuff should clean it with disinfecting wipes just like a regular blood pressure monitor and cuff provided by the facility. When asked if the Sani-Cloth disinfecting wipes provided by the agency were effective for cleaning a soft, porous surface such as the fabric on the cuff of the Wrist Blood Pressure Monitor used by S2, S9 stated she was not sure and would have to look into it. S9 stated, after staff clean a tablet with a Sani-Cloth wipe, the tablet should be allowed to dry for at least one minute before it is returned to the bag.

Cross reference:

NJAC 8:42-12.2(b)(3)

Written notice for non-covered care
CFR(s): 484.50(c)(8)
Receive proper written notice, in advance of a specific service being furnished, if the HHA believes that the service may be non-covered care; or in advance of the HHA reducing or terminating on-going care. The HHA must also comply with the requirements of 42 CFR 405.1200 through 405.1204.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on staff interview, facility document review, and review of medical records, it was determined the facility failed to ensure all patients with Medicare coverage receive a “Notice of Medicare Non-Coverage (NOMNC)” at least two days prior to the date of discharge in four of five discharged Medicare patients (Patients (P) 13, P14, P15, and P16) reviewed. 

 

 

Findings include:

Reference: 42 CFR 405.1200 (b)(1): Timing of notice. A provider must notify the beneficiary of the decision to terminate covered services no later than 2 days before the proposed end of the services. If the beneficiary's services are expected to be fewer than 2 days in duration, the provider must notify the beneficiary at the time of admission to the provider. If, in a non-residential setting, the span of time between services exceeds 2 days, the notice must be given no later than the next to last time services are furnished.

A review of P13’s medical record revealed a “Visit Note Report” dated 03/14/26, which stated, ““…Visit Type:.. PT [Physical Therapy] Discharge from Agency…” A “Client Coordination Note Report” dated 03/17/26, stated, “…Notice of Medicare Provider Non-Coverage was mailed to patient 3/17/26…” This was three days after P13 was discharged. The medical record lacked evidence that P13 received a NOMNC at least two days prior to the date of discharge.

On 06/02/26 at 1:25 PM, Staff (S) 1 explained that after P13’s discharge, it was identified that his/her medical record was missing a NOMNC. S1 reported that once this was identified, the NOMNC was mailed to the patient.

A review of P14’s medical record revealed a “Visit Note Report” dated 03/05/26, which stated, “… Visit Type: ... PT Discharge from Agency…” P14's medical record contained a NOMNC signed by P14's caregiver on 03/05/26, the same day P14 was discharged. The medical record lacked evidence the patient received the NOMNC at least two days prior to the date of P14’s discharge.

On 06/02/26 at 1:25 PM, S1 confirmed P14’s NOMNC was provided on the day of discharge, not at least two days prior.

A review of P15’s medical record revealed the patient was discharged from the Home Health Agency (HHA) on 12/30/25. The medical record lacked evidence the patient received a NOMNC prior to discharge.

On 06/02/26 at 1:25 PM, S1 confirmed P15’s medical record was missing a signed NOMNC.

A review of P16’s medical record revealed a “Client Coordination Note Report” dated, 12/23/25, which stated, “…Note…Patient seen for discharge from agency…” A NOMNC was signed by P16 on 12/23/25, the same day as discharge. The medical record lacked evidence of a signed NOMNC at least two days prior to the date of P16’s discharge.

On 06/02/26 at 2:15 PM, S1 confirmed P16’s NOMNC was signed on the day of discharge, not at least two days prior.

On 06/03/26 at 11:47 AM, a NOMNC policy was requested. S1 reported the facility does not have a NOMNC policy.

source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Conformance with physician orders
CFR(s): 484.60(b)
Standard: Conformance with physician or allowed practitioner orders.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on medical record review, facility policy review, and staff interview, it was determined the facility failed to ensure, that services ordered by the physician are provided, as indicated in the plan of care.

Facility policy titled, “Missed Visits” revised 10/2021, states, “I. Policy Visit patterns are determined during the care planning phase and are included as part of physician orders. Missed visits cause alterations to these visit patterns and physicians should be informed of these changes and the reason for the alteration. II. Procedure: 1. If there is an alteration to the visit pattern causing the visits to fall under the number ordered on the 485 or most recent physician verbal order, the physician should be notified via phone or other method – i.e.. electronic notification, fax, secure email or other agency approved mechanism. The missed visit reason should be included in this communication to the physician and accessible to the interdisciplinary team. …”.

On 2/14/24 during a review of Patient (P)8’s medical record, the “Home Health Certification and Plan of Care" for Patient (P) 8, for the certification period of 12/22/23 to 2/19/24, revealed the following: The section labeled Frequency/Duration of Visits stated, "PT [Physical Therapy] 1WK1, 2EVERY2WK2, 2WK3, 2WK3, 1WK1 [one time a week for one week, two times a week every 2 weeks for 2 weeks, two times a week for three weeks, and once a week for one week]."

The week of 1/14/24, P8’s medical record indicated only one physical therapy visit was made. The “Client Coordination Note Report” dated 1/21/24 states “…Note Type: MISSED VISIT NOTIFICATION. …Note: MUST DOCUMENT IF RESCHEDULING VISIT AND/OR THAT MD HAS BEEN CALLED FOR NOTIFICATION OF ALTERATION IN THE ORDERED VISIT PATTERN (DOCUMENT NAME OF MD CALLED & NAME/TITLE OF WHO YOU SPEAK WITH AT MD OFFICE) SNOWING. “

On 2/15/24 at 2:15PM, S2 (Clinical Director) confirmed that the missed visit notification for the visit scheduled on 1/19/24, by the Physical Therapist, was documented late, on 1/21/24. The missed visit notification did not indicate the physician was aware of the missed visit.

On 2/15/24, during a review of P16’s medical record, the “Home Health Certification and Plan of Care," for the Certification Period of 8/16/2023 through 10/14/2023, revealed the following: “Social [SW] effective 8/20/23 1WK1 [one visit each week for one week]” and the following orders for Home Health Aide visits: “HHA [Home Health Aide] effective 8/20/23 1WK5 [one visit each week for five weeks].

The week of 8/20/23, P16’s medical record indicated that a Social Worker visit was missed. The medical record lacked documentation that a Physician was notified. On 2/15/24 at 1:40 PM, S2 confirmed the medical records lacked documentation that a physician was notified of the missed visit for the week of 8/20/23. 

The week of 8/27/23, P16’s medical record indicated that a Home Health Aide (HHA) visit was missed. A “Missed Visit Notification” entered by the HHA, from 8/30/23, stated, “…Note…PATIENT NO HOME, NO ANSWER FONO [sic].” On 2/15/24 at 11:52 AM, S2 stated, “The HHA would not notify a physician, they would notify the office and the office would notify the physician of the missed visit.” S2 confirmed the medical record lacked evidence the physician was notified of the missed visit from the HHA or from office staff.

On 2/15/23, during a review of P17's medical record, the “Home Health Certification and Plan of Care" revealed the following orders, “…effective 8/27/23 HHA [Home Health Aide] 2WK2 [two visits every week for two weeks], 1WK2 [one visit a week for two weeks] 2WK1 [two visits a week for one week] …”

The week of 8/27/23, P17’s medical record indicated two HHA visits were missed. P17's medical record lacked evidence that the physician was notified of the two missed visits the week of 8/27/2023.

On 2/15/23 at 1:25 PM, during an interview with S2, S2 indicated providers should be notified “within a timely manner.” S2 confirmed the medical record lacked evidence that the physician and/or office staff was notified of the missed visits.

source_record.Facility Name: MERCER CARE PARTNERS MEDICAL HOME HEALTH CARE, LLC
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Infection Prevention
CFR(s): 484.70(a)
Standard: Infection Prevention.  

The HHA must follow accepted standards of practice, including the use of standard precautions, to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation, facility policy review, staff interviews, and nationally recognized guidelines, it was determined the facility failed to provide a sanitary environment by ensuring: 1) proper hand hygiene practices are implemented according to facility policy and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines; 2) proper bag technique practices are implemented according to facility policy.

 

 

Findings include:

1) Reference: The “Guideline for Hand Hygiene in Health Care Settings: Recommendation of the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee [HICPAC] and the HICPAC/SHEA/APIC/IDSA Hand Hygiene Task Force,” published in the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report at MMWR 2002; 51 (No. RR-16) page 32 stated, “Recommendations 1. Indications for handwashing and hand antisepsis: ... I. Decontaminate hands after contact with inanimate objects (including medical equipment) in the immediate vicinity of the patient …” It was determined that the facility practice is not in accordance with the CDC Guideline.

Facility policy titled, “Hand Hygiene” dated 3/21, stated, “… If hands are not visibly soiled … use an alcohol-based hand rub for routinely decontaminating hands in all other clinical situations, … after contact with inanimate objects or known dirty areas, …”

On 2/12/24 at 12:40 PM, Staff (S) 9, an Occupational Therapist (OT), was observed removing a disposable pad from underneath a patient and then rolling it up to throw away, with bare hands. S9 failed to don PPE (Personal Protective Equipment) or perform hand hygiene.

On 2/12/24 at 1:45 PM, S10, a Registered Nurse (RN), was observed touching a patient’s urine leg bag, and failed to perform hand hygiene before opening his/her bag.

2) Facility policy titled, “Bag Technique and Equipment” dated 10/23, stated, “… II. Procedure. … C. Place bag on a clean field (plastic, paper, or newspaper barrier, etc.) or clean surface. Do not place on floor. ... E. Prepare a clean area or use a clean field to lay out equipment or supplies. F. Use hand hygiene before removing contents of the bag. …H. After care is given, clean equipment. …VIII. Management of Electronic Medical Record Devices in the Home. … B. Wipe down Electronic Medical Record devices, i.e., smart phones, tablets, etc. with agency-approved disinfectant wipes, such as alcohol wipes, after completing each patient visit. …”

On 2/12/24 at 12:05 PM, S3 (Home Health Aide), was observed entering the home, verbally greeting the patient (P4), and setting his/her bag on the living room floor. During an interview with S3 at 1:11 PM, S3 indicated that although the facility provides HHA’s with bags for equipment such as Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), the bag he/she was carrying was his/her personal bag.

On 2/15/24 at 1:47 PM, during an interview with S2 (Clinical Director), S2 indicated that bag technique is routinely reviewed with staff; and that all disciplines, including HHA’s, are expected to follow the bag technique and care outlined in the policy. S2 also indicated this applies to any bag carried into the patient’s home; personal or facility issued.    

On 2/14/24 at 9:35 AM, during a home visit of P6, S4 (Registered Nurse) was observed using a blood pressure cuff and scissors for P6 during the visit. When S4 was finished with the dirty items, he/she placed the items down on the disposable pad, he/she then cleaned them using a Micro-Kill One cloth wipe and immediately placed the items back down on the dirty area of the disposable cloth to dry.

On 2/12/24 at 12:40 PM, during an observation with S9, after obtaining vital signs on a patient, S9 was observed picking up the “dirty” blood pressure cuff, cleaning it with a sanitizing wipe, then immediately placing it back into his/her bag. S9 did not utilize a “clean” area, outside of the bag, keeping the dirty and clean equipment separated, nor did he/she allow any time for the blood pressure cuff to dry.

On 2/12/24 at 1:45 PM, during an observation with S10, he/she was observed using the sanitizing wipes to clean the dirty equipment, then placed the cleaned equipment back on the “dirty” area where the used equipment came from. S10 did not wipe down the tablet after the patient used it for a signature. S10 also failed to perform hand hygiene before leaving the patient’s room.

 On 2/15/24 at 2:37 PM, S1(Administrator) and S2 indicated that staff should always utilize two distinct areas; one for clean items and one for dirty items. 

N.J.A.C. 8:42-12.3 (a)4

source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):

CFR(s): 484.60(a)(1)
Each patient must receive the home health services that are written in an individualized plan of care that identifies patient-specific measurable outcomes and goals, and which is established, periodically reviewed, and signed by a doctor of medicine, osteopathy, or podiatry acting within the scope of his or her state license, certification, or registration. This Standard is not met as evidenced by:

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy, "Missed Visits" states, "... If there is an alteration to the visit pattern causing the visits to fall under the number ordered on the 485 or most recent physician verbal order, the physician should be notified via phone or other method... The missed visit reason should be included in this communication to the physician and accessible to the interdisciplinary team."

1. Upon interview on 3/26/21, Staff #2 stated that clinical staff are required to enter missed visit notes in the medical record and notify the physician when visits are missed.

2. Review of Medical Record #7 on 3/26/21 revealed the following:

a. For certification period 12/9/20 - 2/6/21, the Home Health Certification and Plan of Care states, "Frequency/Duration of Visits: HHA (Home Health Aide), 1WK1 (once a week for one week), 2WK4 (twice a week for four weeks)... ."

c. Review of HHA visits for week 12/13/20 - 12/19/20 revealed one (1) HHA visit made on 12/14/20. The plan of care called for two (2) HHA visits to be made this week.

(i) There was no evidence of a missed visit note in the medical record indicating why the visit was missed.
