source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1): This report is the result of an unannounced standard-level Federal Recertification and State Re-licensure Survey completed on May 1, 2025, at Hackensack Meridian at Home - Monmouth County. It was determined the facility is not in substantial compliance with Federal requirements of 42 CFR Part 484, Subpart B Conditions of Participation for Home Health Agencies and State requirements of N.J.A.C. Title 8 Chapter 42 Home Health Agency Licensing Standards.

Infection Prevention
CFR(s): 484.70(a)
Standard: Infection Prevention.  

The HHA must follow accepted standards of practice, including the use of standard precautions, to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observations, staff interview, and a review of facility policies, it was determined the facility failed to follow the facility policy to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases, in four of seven home visit patients (Patient (P)1, P3, P4, and P6).

Findings include:

On 4/30/25 at 9:19 AM, during a home visit with Patient (P) 4, in the presence of Staff (S)10 (Licensed Practical Nurse) and S11 (Manager of Clinical Practice), S10 was observed setting up his/her laptop computer on a clean barrier on the patient's table. At 9:25 AM, while speaking with the patient, S10 was then observed walking around the table, touching and adjusting the backs of the chairs, prior to using the laptop computer. S10 was not observed performing hand hygiene before using the laptop computer. The computer was not disinfected after use. 

At 1:46 PM, during an interview with S4 (Director of Quality), he/she provided documentation of their procedure for cleaning the laptop computers. Review of facility document titled "Procedure for Care, Cleaning, and Infection Prevention Practices for the Computer and Other Electronic Devices" revealed the following: ".Purpose: ...Electronic devices include, but are limited to, computers, tablets, and mobile phones. ..Care and Cleansing of the Computer/Electronic Device:. All electronic devices should be disinfected daily when visibly soiled or contaminated. ...Special instructions: Always remove gloves and perform hand hygiene before touching all electronic devices, including the computer, screen, keyboard, stylus, and mouse. ..." S4 confirmed that the laptops are cleaned at the end of each day, and that staff are to perform hand hygiene prior to using the laptop computer. At 2:01 PM, S4 confirmed that when S10 touched the chairs in P4's home, the expectation was that S10 would perform hand hygiene prior to using the laptop. 

Findings include:

Facility policy titled "Hand Washing and Hand Hygiene", last revised on 07/2024, stated, “Policy: … hand hygiene will be performed in accordance with the CDC guidelines … cleaning your hands by using either handwashing with soap and water or antiseptic hand rub with alcohol-based hand sanitizer … Procedure: Hands are a common transfer mechanism for potential pathogens from one patient to another, from a contaminated article from the patient or patient’s environment or from healthcare personnel to the patient … C. Hand Washing/Hand Hygiene Indications: … Before and after contact with patient or environment …”

Facility undated policy titled “Cleaning & Disinfecting Guidelines for Patient Care Equipment, stated, “Policy: … has been established to prevent the transmission of pathologic organisms between patients and caregivers … Procedure: 1. Thermometer, stethoscope (bell) and pulse oximeter: Cleaned between each patient use … 2. … non-critical items, including, but not limited to, blood pressure cuffs … must be cleaned/disinfected after use on patient … 3. Separation must be maintained between clean and soiled equipment to prevent cross-contamination …” 

Facility policy titled "Bag Technique", last revised on 03/2022, stated, “… 5. Remove supplies from clean area … and place on the clean barrier … 12. Clean equipment per policy prior to returning it to the clinician bag …” 

Facility undated policy titled "Procedure for Care, Cleaning, and Infection Prevention Practices for the Computer & Other Electronic Devices", stated, “Care and Cleansing of the Computer/Electronic Device: All electronic devices should be disinfected daily and when … contaminated … Special Instructions: Always remove gloves and perform hand hygiene before touching all electronic devices, including the computer …”

On 04/29/25 at 11:35 AM, in the presence of Staff (S)8 (Therapy Supervisor), S12, an Occupational Therapist (OT) was observed providing care for P6.

At 11:14 AM, while completing a medication reconciliation with P6’s spouse, S12 touched medication bottles and then proceeded to touch his/her computer without washing and/or sanitizing his/her hands multiple times. 

At 11:51 AM, S12 touched P6's arm and then proceeded to touch his/her computer without washing and/or sanitizing his/her hands.

At 12:07 PM, S12 completed vital signs on P6. During this process, S12 touched P6 multiple times and then proceeded to touch his/her computer without washing and/or sanitizing his/her hands. 

At 12:14 PM, S12 closed and picked up his/her computer, without cleaning the computer, and proceeded to exit the home. 

On 04/30/25 at 12:15 PM, in the presence of S8, S15, a Physical Therapist (PT) was observed providing care for P1.

At 11:18 AM, S15 placed three barrier pads on P1's dresser for patient care. S15's laptop and paperwork were placed on the left barrier pad.

At 11:20 AM, while completing a medication reconciliation with P1’s private aide, the private aide handed S15 a plastic bin filled with medications. S15 placed the medications on center barrier pad. While S15 was reviewing the medications with his/her computer, P1's private aid placed papers on the right barrier pad. 

At 11:22 AM, S15 completed a set of vital signs for P1 utilizing the following equipment: blood pressure cuff, pulse oximeter, thermometer, and stethoscope. S15 placed dirty equipment on the center barrier pad. 

At 11:25 AM, S15 utilized disinfectant wipes to clean the equipment (blood pressure cuff, pulse oximeter, thermometer, and stethoscope). S15 placed clean equipment on the right barrier pad to dry.

At 11:58 AM, S15 set up P1’s next appointments for physical therapy and updated a dry erase board calendar. 

At 12:01 PM, P1’s private aid placed the updated dry erase board calendar on top of the clean equipment on the right barrier pad.

At 12:05 PM, S15 placed the equipment back in the nursing bag without re-cleaning the equipment.

At 12:06 PM, S15 closed and picked up his/her computer, without cleaning the computer, and proceeded to exit the home.

On 05/01/25 at 12:02 PM, an interview was conducted with S19 (Staff Development). When questioned about infection control related to bag technique, S19 explained that during orientation, new staff are trained on infection control, which includes bag technique. S19 further explained that all staff members review bag technique on a yearly basis. S19 stated that if an item that is considered dirty is placed on the clean barrier with already cleaned supplies, then the supplies would be required to be re-cleaned. When questioned about infection control related to staff computers, S19 stated, "We tell staff to think of your computer as always clean because you wash your hands before you touch it." S19 explained that computers are not cleaned during every visit since they are only touched with cleaned hands; instead, they are cleaned at the end of every week. S19 revealed that staff are trained on the “Procedure for Care, Cleaning, and Infection Prevention Practices for the Computer & Other Electronic Devices” policy during orientation and then every three years.

Cross reference:

NJAC 8:42-12.2(b)

On 04/30/25 at 9:32 AM, in the presences of Staff (S) 6 (Manager of Clinical Practice), S5, Registered Nurse (RN) was observed providing care for P3.

At 9:35 AM, S5 spoke with P3's spouse regarding P3's medications, glucose (sugar) levels, diet, balance, pain, and upcoming schedule for the week. 

At 10:02 AM, S5 placed a barrier pad on P3's table and placed the nursing bag on the barrier pad. S5 performed hand hygiene and placed a second barrier down on the table. S5 removed "Super Sani Cloth" (germicidal wipes) and placed the wipes and the hand sanitizer on the second barrier. 

At 10:06 AM, S5 began vital sign assessment on P3. 

At 10:12 AM, S5 finished taking P3's vital signs and began cleaning the equipment with a "Super Sani Cloth." After using the disinfectant wipes on the vital sign equipment (stethoscope, pulse oximeter, and blood pressure cuff), S5 placed the clean equipment onto the barrier where the hand sanitizer and "Super Sani Cloth" were located. 

At 10:14 AM, S5 began to drain P3's pleurx catheter (a tube placed into the body to drain excess fluid) and when finished draining, S5 changed P3's dressing. 

At 10:28 AM, S5 performed hand sanitized and repeated P3's vital signs.

at 10:36 AM, S5 cleaned the equipment with a "Super Sani Cloth" and placed the clean equipment onto the second barrier on top of the "Super Sani Cloth" package. 

On 04/30/25 at 10:16 AM, S6 stated that "Super Sani Cloths" are contained within the "dirty" section of the nursing bag. 

On 05/01/25 at 12:03 PM, the observed nursing procedure during P3's home visit was described to S19 (Staff Development). S19 explained that clean vital signs equipment should not have been placed on the barrier with the hand sanitizer and the "Super Sani Cloth" and he/she stated, "oh no, you need a whole separate barrier, at least 5-6 per visit."  When asked if the "Super Sani Cloth" were considered "dirty" S 19 stated that they are clean and kept in the "clean" section of the nursing bag. 

Facility policy, titled, "Bag Technique," last revised 03/2022, states, "...Bag Setup...Small Side Zipper Area (A): The "dirty" section. Meridian provided soap, Epiclenz gel, paper towels, alcohol swabs, Sani-Wipes, Gluco-chlor wipes, Barriers....Main Zipper Area (B): The "Clean Section." All dressing supplies, foleys, blood tubing, clean gloves, suture removal kits, single use thermometers, OSHA bag, spill kit, and any clean supplies needed for patient care..."

RN performs assessment
CFR(s): 484.55(a)(1)
A registered nurse must conduct an initial assessment visit to determine the immediate care and support needs of the patient; and, for Medicare patients, to determine eligibility for the Medicare home health benefit, including homebound status. The initial assessment visit must be held either within 48 hours of referral, or within 48 hours of the patient's return home, or on the physician or allowed practitioner - ordered start of care date.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on medical record review, interviews with staff, and review of facility documents, it was determined the facility failed to follow facility policy to conduct initial assessments with 48 hours of referral, or within 48 hours of the patient’s return home, or on the physician-ordered start of care date in three of five medical records reviewed (Patient (P)6, 11, and 14).

Findings include:

Facility policy titled “Initial and Comprehensive Assessments” last revised 03/2022 states “Purpose: To provide guidelines for the initial assessments of patients admitted to service… Policy: … The initial assessment visit must be performed either within 48 hours of the referral, within 48 hours of patient’s discharge from inpatient, on the start of care date ordered by the physician (or other licensed practitioner), at the patient/family request with the approval of the physician (or other licensed practitioner) or within 48 hours of the organization receiving notification of patient’s return home on resumption of care. …”

On 5/1/25 at 9:30 AM, a review of P6’s medical record was conducted with Staff (S)6 (Registered Nurse (RN) / Manager of Clinical Practice) and S18 (Clinical Director of Ocean County) and revealed the following:

On 3/20/25, P6 received a referral from a physician for home health care.

On 4/5/25, P6 was discharged to home from the hospital.

On 4/8/25 at 11:20 AM, telephone communication from S6 to P6’s caregiver stated that P6 was “home ok” and agreeable to SOC (start of care).

On 4/10/25 at 12:22 PM, RN conducted initial assessment of P6.

On 5/1/25 at 10:09 AM, a review of P11’s medical record was conducted with S6 and S18 and revealed the following:

On 3/17/25, P11 received a referral from a physician for home health care.

On 3/17/25, P11 was discharged to home from the hospital.

On 3/18/25 at 4:30 PM, a telephone communication to the patient stated the facility “LVM (left voicemail) to set up HC (home care) svcs (services).”

On 3/20/25 at 11:57 AM, a telephone communication to the patient stated “home and agreeable to SOC. All information verified.”

On 3/27/25 at 11:07 AM, RN conducted an initial assessment of P11.

On 5/1/25 at 10:25 AM, S6 and S18 confirmed that there were no additional communication notes between 3/20/25 and 3/27/25 to explain the delay in the initial assessment.

On 5/1/25 at 10:28 AM, a review of P14’s medical record was conducted with S6 and S18 and revealed the following:

On 11/5/24, P14’s referral from a physician for home health care was initiated.

On 11/6/24, P14 was discharged to home from the hospital.

On 11/7/24, physician signed the referral for P14.

On 11/8/24 at 11:40 AM, a telephone communication to P14’s daughter stated that P14 was home and “agreeable to SOC.”

On 11/10/24 at 12:06 PM, RN conducted an initial assessment of P14.

On 5/1/25 at 10:34 AM, when questioned about when P14 should have received an initial assessment per facility policy, S6 stated that “P14 should have been seen on 11/9/24.” S6 and S18 confirmed that there were no additional notes to explain the delay in receiving the initial assessment.

Cross Reference:

NJAC 8:42-6.1(a)3 - Plan of Care

Communication with all physicians
CFR(s): 484.60(d)(1)
Standard: Coordination of Care. The HHA must: 
(1) Assure communication with all physicians or allowed practitioners involved in the plan of care.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on medical record review, staff interview, and review of facility policies, it was determined the facility failed to ensure communication with the physician is documented when a delay in services, due to staffing, occurrs, in one of five medical records reviewed (Patient (P)2).

Findings include:

Facility policy titled "Verification of Physician Orders", last revised on 03/2022, states, "Notices To The Physician: ... 2. If fewer visits are provided during the week than ordered, the physician will be notified with documentation in the clinical record that the physician is aware of the missed visit unless the physician has authorized missed visits under specific circumstances …" 

On 04/30/25 at 2:29 PM, a review of P2's medical record was conducted with Staff (S)6 (Registered Nurse/Manager Clinical Practice) and S18 (Clinical Director Ocean County) and revealed the following:

A review of P2's "Home Health Plan of Care" document, for the certification period beginning 3/10/25, showed visit orders for the Home Health Aide (HHA) as “… Aide (HHA) 2 visits every week for 1 week from 3/10/25 to 3/15/25."

During the week of 03/10/25 to 03/15/25, P2 was only visited once by the HHA on 03/12/25.

On 03/13/2025, a Home Health Aide (HHA) note documented a missed visit for P2. The note explained that P2's spouse cancelled the appointment after he/she arrived at the home. There was no documented method of notification to the physician (verbal or fax) for the missed visit in the medical record.

On 04/30/25 at 2:42 PM, the findings were confirmed by S6 and S18. When questioned regarding the missed visit, S18 stated, "The doctor is always notified regardless of reason for the missed visit."

Cross reference:

NJAC 8:42-6.1(a)3 - Care Plans

Must have a written agreement
CFR(s): 484.105(e)(2)(i-iv)
An HHA must have a written agreement with another agency, with an organization, or with an individual when that entity or individual furnishes services under arrangement to the HHA's patients.  The HHA must maintain overall responsibility for the services provided under arrangement, as well as the manner in which they are furnished. The agency, organization, or individual providing services under arrangement may not have been:

(i) Denied Medicare or Medicaid enrollment;

(ii) Been excluded or terminated from any federal health care program or Medicaid;

(iii) Had its Medicare or Medicaid billing privileges revoked; or

(iv) Been debarred from participating in any government program.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on staff interview and review of facility documents, it was determined the facility failed to ensure a written agreement is in place for social work services provided by a separately certified Home Health Agency (HHA).

Findings Include:

On 4/29/25 on 9:49 AM, during a review of services offered by the Home Care, Staff (S) 2 (Director of Home Care) reported that the facility did not utilize any contracted services.

On 5/1/25 at 9:30 AM, the medical record revealed that Patient (P)6 was seen by social worker on 4/12/25.  

On 5/1/25 at 9:53 AM, during medical record review, S20 (Clinical Director), in the presence of S19 (Staff Development), reported that the facility’s only social worker was on medical leave.

On 5/1/25 at 12:15 PM, a review of the facility’s staff list revealed only one social worker is employed by the HHA.

On 5/1/25 at 12:39 PM, an interview was conducted with S2 and S3 (Vice President of Home Care). S2 explained that the HHA employs one social worker, and he/she is currently on a medical leave. According to S2, the Social Worker began medical leave in mid-March. S2 explained that the Ocean County HHA is providing social work coverage. According to S2, when a patient has a social work referral, the scheduling department contacts the director of Ocean County HHA to confirm social work availability before placing the patient on the Ocean County social worker’s caseload. S2 reported that if the consult is urgent, this is communicated during scheduling. S3 explained that the social worker job description, electronic medical record, and training, at both HHAs is the same. S2 reported there are currently 17 patients being followed by social work.

Upon request, the facility failed to provide a written agreement between the two HHAs. On 5/1/25 at 1:30 PM, S22 (Senior Vice President) confirmed the facility does not have a written agreement regarding the use of social work services from the Ocean County HHA. 

 

Cross Reference:

NJAC 8:42-3.7(a) - Written Agreements

source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
A Federal Recertification survey was conducted on September 9, 10, and 11, 2019, which resulted in Standard Level deficiencies.

Home visits: 5

Medical records reviewed: 8

Staff files reviewed/staff interviewed: 10

Infection Prevention
CFR(s): 484.70(a)
Standard: Infection Prevention.  

The HHA must follow accepted standards of practice, including the use of standard precautions, to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:

Based on observation, staff interview, and review of facility policy and procedure, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that all staff adhere to the use of standard precautions with acceptable standards of practice to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases. 

Findings include:

Reference #1: Facility policy titled, "Integumentary - Application of Wound Dressing" states, "... Procedure: 1. Adhere to Standard Precautions. ... 4. Establish a clean field ... with all the supplies and equipment that will be necessary. 5. ... Remove soiled dressing. Discard dressing and gloves ... . Decontaminate hands and don clean gloves. ..." 

1. On 9/9/19, a home visit for Patient #1 was conducted. While performing a dressing change to the patient's upper chest wound, the following was observed:

a. Staff #5 donned (put on) gloves and prepared a clean field with supplies. The supplies placed onto the clean field included a pile of unwrapped 4x4 gauze and the large supply pack of the unwrapped 4x4 gauze. 

(i) Staff #5 removed the upper chest wound dressing. While wearing the same gloves, Staff #5 utilized the 4x4 gauze that was placed on the clean field and then reached into the large supply of clean gauze to retrieve additional gauze to complete the dressing. 

(ii) Staff #5 did not discard her/his gloves or sanitize hands prior to retrieving more gauze from the clean supply sleeve contaminating the supply. 

2. The above findings were confirmed by Staff #1, Staff #4 and Staff #5.

Communication with all physicians
CFR(s): 484.60(d)(1)
Assure communication with all physicians involved in the plan of care.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:

Based on staff interview, medical record review, and review of facility policies and procedures, it was determined that the facility failed to communicate with the physician involved in the plan of care.

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy titled, "Verification of Physician Orders" states, "... Notices to the Physician. ... 1. The office will notify the physician if the patient refuses service or treatment ordered and will document that refusal in the clinical record. ... 2. If fewer visits are provided during the week then ordered, the physician will be notified with documentation in the clinical record that the physician is aware of the missed visit unless the physician has authorized missed visits under specific circumstances. ..."

1. On 9/11/19, a review of Medical Record #7 revealed the following:

a. The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care, Start of Care dated 6/25/19, for the Certification Period 6/25/19 to 8/23/19 indicated skilled nursing visits for the week of 6/30/19 2x1Wx1W [2 visits in one week for one week]. 

(i) Medical Record #7 lacked documentation of any skilled nursing visits for the week of 6/30/19.

(ii) A Memo dated 7/2/19, from a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) indicated that the patient was unavailable for a skilled nurse visit that day.

(iii) A Memo dated 7/5/19, from a Registered Nurse (RN) indicated that the patient's wife declined a skilled nurse visit that day.

b. There was no documentation in the medical record of communication to the patient's physician of the missed skilled nurse visits.

c. The above was confirmed by Staff #1.

2. In Medical Record #6, the Home Health Certification and Plan of Treatment for certification period 6/6/19 to 8/4/19 indicated an order for Physical Therapy (PT) beginning 6/7/19 for 1x6Dx6D [1 visit, in 6 days, for 6 days]. 

a. Review of the medical record revealed that there were no PT visits conducted within the six (6) day period starting 6/7/19. 

(i) There was no documentation regarding the missed visit. 

b. There was no documentation in the medical record of communication to the patient's physician of the missed PT visit.

3. The above findings were confirmed by Staff #1.

source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Provide services in the plan of care
CFR(s): 484.75(b)(3)
Providing services that are ordered by the physician as indicated in the plan of care;

This Element is not met as evidenced by:

Based on observation, staff interview, and review of facility documents, it was determined that the facility failed to provide services indicated in the plan of care.

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy titled, "Infusion Therapy - Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter (PICC) Maintenance and Management of Potential Complications" states, "... D. Dressing Change ... Procedure: ... 6. Don non-sterile gloves and mask. 7. Slowly loosen transparent dressing at the distal end while anchoring catheter with the other hand. ... 14. Measure external catheter length from exit point of the skin to the hub. Compare initial insertion measurement. If there is greater than a 2 cm discrepancy, report to physician as the PICC line tip location requires additional evaluation before using with drug or fluid administration."

1. Review of Medical Record #2 on 9/10/19 revealed the following:

b. The Home Health Certification and Plan of Care for certification period 6/6/19 to 10/4/19 stated, "... Care Plan ... Infusion - Home Care ... Goals ... picc will remain patent without s/s [signs and symptoms] of infection, infiltration, and/or phlebitis until removed ... Interventions ... PICC length 20 cm ..."

2. On 9/10/19, during a home visit of Patient #2, Staff #10 performed a central line dressing change. 

a. Staff #10 failed to don (put on) a mask, prior to removal of the central line dressing. 

b. After performing the central line dressing, Staff #10 failed to measure the external catheter length and compare to initial measurement to ensure that there was no discrepancy. 

3. The above findings were confirmed by Staff #3.

source_record.Deficiency Description: Initial Comments - Not A Deficiency Citation
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1): This report is the result of an unannounced standard-level Federal Recertification and State Relicensure Survey completed on May 6, 2026 at Bayada at Inspira, Home Health and Hospice. It was determined the facility is not in substantial compliance with Federal requirements of 42 CFR Part 484, Subpart B Conditions of Participation for Home Health Agencies and State requirements of N.J.A.C. Title 8 Chapter 42 Home Health Agency Licensing Standards.

HHA Comprehensive Assessment in Disaster
CFR(s): 484.102(b)(1)
§484.102(b)(1) Condition for Participation:

[(b) Policies and procedures.  The HHA must develop and implement emergency preparedness policies and procedures, based on the emergency plan set forth in paragraph (a) of this section, risk assessment at paragraph (a)(1) of this section, and the communication plan at paragraph (c) of this section.  The policies and procedures must be reviewed and updated at least every 2 years. 

At a minimum, the policies and procedures must address the following:]



(1) The plans for the HHA's patients during a natural or man-made disaster. Individual plans for each patient must be included as part of the comprehensive patient assessment, which must be conducted according to the provisions at §484.55.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation, medical record review, staff interview, and review of facility policy, it was determined the facility failed to ensure individual emergency preparedness plans are developed in three of six medical records reviewed (Patients (P) 3, P4, and P5).

Findings include:

Facility policy titled, "0-9197 Emergency Management Program and Plan – Medicare-Certified Offices," dated 02/06/25, stated, "… Our Procedure: … 4.0 Standards for Emergency Management Planning … 4.1.3 Client-Specific Emergency Plans. At admission, all clients will be educated on the risks of disasters and the importance of emergency planning. 4.1.3.1 As part of the comprehensive assessment, the admitting clinician will develop a Client- Specific Emergency Plan by entering the information into the electronic record and also using 0-9236 – Client -Specific Emergency Plan – Home Health and Hospice … The Client- Specific Emergency Plan will include specific instructions for the client …"  

On 05/04/26 at 1:45 PM, Staff (S) 9 was observed completing a home visit for P3. 

At 1:59 PM, a review of P3's admission packet was conducted with S9. A blank "Client-Specific Emergency Plan – Home Health and Hospice Offices" form was observed in the admission packet. The admission packet lacked evidence of a completed individual emergency preparedness plan.   

At 2:31 PM, an interview was conducted with S9. S9 confirmed P3 did not have a completed individual emergency preparedness plan in his/her admission packet. S9 stated the individual emergency preparedness plan should be completed at the start of care and should be both on paper and electronic, in the patient's medical record. 

On 05/06/26, a review of P3, P4, and P5's medical record was conducted and revealed the following:

For the start of care beginning on 02/09/26 and the recertification period beginning on 04/10/26, P3's medical record lacked evidence of an individual emergency preparedness plan.

For the start of care beginning 03/26/26, P4's medical record lacked evidence of an individual emergency preparedness plan.

For the start of care beginning 04/14/26, P5's medical record lacked evidence of an individual emergency preparedness plan.

On 05/06/26 at 1:16 PM, an interview was conducted with S1, S2, and S3. S1 stated an individualized emergency preparedness plan is completed for each patient during the start of care, resumption of care, recertification, and if there is a change in the plan. S3 stated all emergency preparedness plans should be uploaded to the patient's electronic medical record. S1 stated that registered nurses, physical therapists, and speech-language pathologists are able to complete the patient's emergency preparedness plan.

At 2:27 PM, an interview was conducted with S3. S3 confirmed P3, P4, and P5 did not have a completed individual emergency preparedness plan in their electronic medical records.  

Cross reference: 

NJAC 8:42-6.1(a)(7)

Written notice for non-covered care
CFR(s): 484.50(c)(8)
Receive proper written notice, in advance of a specific service being furnished, if the HHA believes that the service may be non-covered care; or in advance of the HHA reducing or terminating on-going care. The HHA must also comply with the requirements of 42 CFR 405.1200 through 405.1204.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation, staff interview, facility document review, and review of medical records, it was determined the facility failed to ensure that all patients with Medicare coverage received a Notice of Medicare Non-Coverage (NOMNC) no later than two days prior to discharge, as per facility policy, for three of six discharged Medicare patients (Patients (P)4, P14, and P16).

On 05/04/26 at 3:14 PM, Staff (S) 6 was observed, in the presence of S10, completing a discharge from agency home visit for P4. 

At 3:54 PM, P4 was observed signing a paper NOMNC form. 

At 4:06 PM, P4 was observed signing an electronic NOMNC form on a computer tablet. 

At 4:24 PM, an interview was conducted with S6. When asked about the NOMNC being signed the day of the discharge from the agency, S6 stated that it is usually filled out at least 48 hours prior to discharge, but this wasn't possible since the patient is only seen once a week. S6 explained that P4 saw a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) during the previous week's visit and that the NOMNC wasn't completed at that time because only Registered Nurse's (RN) can complete NOMNC's. 

A review of P4's medical record was conducted and revealed the following:

On 05/04/26, P4 was discharged from Home Care services by S6. The NOMNC was completed on 05/04/26 and signed by P4, less than two days prior to discharge. 

Findings include:

Facility Policy titled, “0-322 Home Health Change of Care Notice (HHCCN), Advanced Beneficiary Notice of Non-Coverage (ABN), Notice of Medicare Non-Coverage (NOMNC) and Fast Track Appeal Review Procedures” dated January 1, 2025, stated “… Our Procedure: …3.0: Notice of Medicare Noncoverage (NOMNC). 3.1: A standardized Review Notice, NOTICE OF MEDICARE NON-COVERAGE (NOMNC), #0-3195, is given on paper or electronically, to all beneficiaries when Medicare coverage is about to end based on the physician’s orders and all home healthcare is ending, (except those admitted to a facility or hospital) no later than two (2) days prior to discharge…3.2: The Initial Notice of Medicare Provider Non-Coverage is delivered as follows: a. Face to face and signed and dated by the client and representative, b. If the Initial Notice of Medicare Provider Non-Coverage cannot or will not be signed, a notation is made on the notice explaining why and dated… 5.0: Retention Requirements: The original notice(s) must be retained in the client’s chart…”

On 05/05/26, a review of P14 and P16’s medical records was conducted and revealed the following:

On 05/15/25, P14 was discharged from Home Care services by Staff (S)12. The NOMNC was completed on 05/15/25 and signed by P14, less than two days prior to discharge.

On 11/13/25, P14 was discharged from Home Care services by S18. The NOMNC was completed on 11/13/25 and signed by P14, less than two days prior discharge.

On 03/09/26, P16 was discharged from Home Care services by S5. P16’s electronic medical record (EMR) lacked evidence of a NOMNC. 

On 05/05/26 at 2:30 PM, an interview was conducted with S1, S2, and S3. When asked about the process for discharge, S1 stated that the NOMNC is provided to the client 48 hours prior to discharge. S1 stated, the signed NOMNC is then uploaded to the EMR by the clinician.  

At 3:23 PM, S3 confirmed that the NOMNC for P14’s discharges on 05/15/25 and 11/13/15 had both been completed on the same date as discharge and should have been completed at least two days prior to discharge. S3 confirmed that the NOMNC for P16 had not been uploaded to the EMR per facility policy.

source_record.Deficiency Description: Initial Comments - Not A Deficiency Citation
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
This was a Federal Recertification Survey conducted on November 29, November 30, December 1, and December 2, 2021. Bayada at Inspira Home Health is not in compliance with 42 CFR Part 484, Subpart B requirements, for Home Health Agencies.

 

As a result of this survey, Standard level deficiencies were cited.

Plan of care
CFR(s): 484.60(a)(1)
Each patient must receive the home health services that are written in an individualized plan of care that identifies patient-specific measurable outcomes and goals, and which is established, periodically reviewed, and signed by a doctor of medicine, osteopathy, or podiatry acting within the scope of his or her state license, certification, or registration. If a physician or allowed practitioner refers a patient under a plan of care that cannot be completed until after an evaluation visit, the physician or allowed practitioner is consulted to approve additions or modifications to the original plan.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on a medical record review for six (6) patients (Patient #3, #5, #6, #7, #8, #15), review of facility policy and procedure, and staff interview, it was determined the facility failed to implement the Plan of Care and their policy and procedure for missed visits for one (1) out of six (6) patients (#8).  

Findings include: 

Reference: Facility Policy titled, "0-6277 Missed Visits/Hours" states, "... . Our policy: Bayada Home Health Care has a process for communication and documentation related to missed visits/hours that are not provided at the frequency stated on the plan of care. Our Procedure: 1.0 Communication missed visits/hours. 1.1 Physician ordered services-The Physician must be notified when the plan of care is altered due to fewer visits or hours of service being provided as ordered. Notification of the missed visits/hours is timely, and as directed on a schedule determined in collaboration with the Physician. ... . 1.1.1.2 Missed visit process flow-Field clinician is responsible for documenting the missed visit in the "Missed Visit Coordination Note" found in the electronic record. ... ." 

1. On 12/2/21, upon medical record review, the following was indicated: 

a. The Plan of Care for Patient #8 was reviewed for the Certification Period 9/4/21 through 11/2/21. The Start of Care date was 9/4/21. 

(i)  The Frequency/Duration of Visits per Physician Order state, "PT [Physical Therapy] 1 WK 1 [one time per week for one week], 2 WK 3 [two times per week for three weeks], and 1 Wk 3 [one time per week for three weeks] ... ."

b. On 12/2/21 at 2:10 PM, upon interview, Staff #2 stated that the agency's calendar week begins on Sundays.  

c. Patient #8 had one (1) PT visit for the week of 9/19/21; there should have been two (2) visits.  

(i) There was no documentation in the medical record of the missed visit for that week or Physician notification.  

2. The above was confirmed by Staff #2.

N.J.A.C 8:42-13.1(b)(6)

Conformance with physician orders
CFR(s): 484.60(b)
Standard: Conformance with physician or allowed practitioner orders.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on medical record review, staff interview and document review, it was determined that the facility failed to implement the Plan of Care.

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy titled, "Missed Visits/Hours" states, "Our Procedure: 1.0 Communicating Missed Visits/Hours. 1.1 Physician Ordered Services. The physician must be notified when the plan of care is altered due to fewer visits or hours of service being provided as ordered. Notification of the missed visits/hours is timely, and as directed on a schedule determined in collaboration with the physician. 1.1.1. 1 Missed Visit Notification note to capture the reason that the visit was missed as well as evidence that the physician was informed verbally or by fax...of this variation from the plan of care must be entered in the electronic record 1.1.1.2 Missed Visit Process Flow. Field clinician is responsible for documenting the missed visit in the "Missed Visit Coordination Note" found in the electronic record. ..."

1. Review of Medical Record #2 on 12/1/21, revealed the following:

a. The Plan of Care states " PT [Physical Therapist] 2WK3" [two times per week for three weeks].

(i) During the week of 10/31/21, there was a missed Physical Therapy visit.

(ii)  There was no evidence that the Physician was notified of the missed visit.

(iii)  There was no evidence that a Missed Visit Coordination Note was completed.

b. The Plan of Care states, "OT [Occupational Therapy] effective 11/07/2021 1WK1 [once per week for one week]."

(i)  There was no OT visit during the week of 11/7/21. 

(ii) On 12/1/21 at 1:50 PM, upon interview, Staff #14 stated that the OT visit was rescheduled to the following week. 

(iv) There was no evidence of a Missed Visit Coordination note to indicate the reason the visit was rescheduled.

2. Review of Medical Record #11 on 12/1/21, revealed the following:

a. The Plan of Care states, "SN [Skilled Nurse] 2WK2 [two times per week for two weeks]."

(i) There was only one (1) SN visit conducted during the week of 9/26/21.

b. On 12/2/21 at 1130 AM, upon interview, Staff #14 stated that during the week of 9/26/21, the Skilled Nurse visit was cancelled.

(i) There was no evidence that the Physician was notified of the missed visit. 

(ii) There was no evidence of a Missed Visit Coordination note.

3. The above findings were confirmed by Staff #14.

N.J.A.C. 8:42-6.2(a)2

Infection Prevention
CFR(s): 484.70(a)
Standard: Infection Prevention.  

The HHA must follow accepted standards of practice, including the use of standard precautions, to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation, review of facility policies and procedures, and staff interviews, it was determined the facility failed to ensure infection prevention procedures are implemented when using Point of Care Devices and that Equipment and Supplies are being cleaned and disinfected in accordance with the organization policy and procedure for one (1) of (5) five observed visits. 

 

 Findings include:

Reference #1: Facility Policy and Procedure titled, "0-4858 Infection Prevention Procedures for Point of Care Devices" states, "... . Our Procedure: Point of care devices require specific Infection Prevention procedures as categorized by device type and location of device below to ensure the safety of the client and employee. ... . a. Point of Care Devices-Tablet or phone used to electronically document client care and visit verification. ... . 3.4 Disinfect tablet or phone using an approved EPA registered disinfectant wipe, and stylus using 70 % isopropyl alcohol wipe or EPA registered disinfectant wipe with gloved hands, at the following times: 3.4.1 Beginning of visit, before returning device to supply bag, and more frequently as needed, if contaminated. ... . 3.4.2 Before and after client visit verification signature. 3.4.2.1 Client finger-Disinfect tablet screen before and after client touches the screen to sign for the visit with a manufacturer's approved EPA registered disinfectant wipe following manufacturer's recommended contact time. ... ."

Reference #2: Facility Policy and Procedure titled, "0-1570 Equipment and Supplies Maintenance" states, "1.0 General Information. 1.1 Handle client care equipment in a manner that prevents skin and mucous membrane exposure , contamination of clothing, and exposure to other environments. Gloves must be worn for cleaning or disinfecting of equipment. ... . 2.1 Non-critical items: ... . These items can undergo a low level of disinfection using isopropyl or ethyl alcohol (70-90 %); germicidal wipes; 1:100 dilution of bleach and water; germicidal detergent solutions... . Examples of non-critical items include, but are not limited to : ... . e. stethoscope; f. blood pressure apparatus; ... .j. pulse oximeters. ... ."

Reference #3: Facility Policy and Procedure titled, "0-1169 Hand Hygiene" states, "... .1.0 Indications for hand decontamination. ... . a. Before and after having any direct client contact with clients ... . Between contact with the environment and the client ... ."

 

1. On 11/30/21 at 1:25 PM, during a home visit for Patient #6, the following was noted:

 

a. During the Home Health Visit, Staff #9 assessed vital signs of Patient #6 with gloved hands. He/she used a stethoscope, blood pressure apparatus and pulse oximeter for the assessment. He /she then doffed (removed) gloves, applied hand sanitizer, and proceeded to wipe down all equipment with un-gloved hands, using an agency supplied alcohol wipe.

(i) Staff #9 did not don (put on) gloves for cleaning of the above equipment. 

 

b. At the conclusion of the visit, Staff #9 asked Patient #6 to sign for verification of the visit on the electronic tablet device. Patient #6 touched the electronic tablet device with fingers, completed the signature, then returned the tablet to Staff #9 . 

(i) Staff #9 placed the tablet under his/her arm pit against his/her clothing and walked out to his/her car without disinfecting the tablet.

(ii) Staff #9 did not perform hand hygiene prior to exiting the home at the conclusion of the visit. 

(iii)  With bare hands, Staff #9 wiped the tablet with an alcohol wipe outside at his/her car.

2. The above findings were reviewed with and confirmed by Staff #9 at the conclusion of the visit.

N.J.A.C. 8:42-12.2 (b)(6)(i) 

N.J.A.C 8:42-12.3(a)(4)

Authentication
CFR(s): 484.110(b)
Standard:  Authentication.  

All entries must be legible, clear, complete, and appropriately authenticated, dated, and timed. Authentication must include a signature and a title (occupation), or a secured computer entry by a unique identifier, of a primary author who has reviewed and approved the entry.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on review of three (3) of seventeen (17) medical records, staff interview and document review, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that all physician orders are authenticated.

Findings include:

Reference #1 Facility policy titled, "0-986 Communicating With Physicians" states, "...4.0 Skilled Cases. 4.1 A home health Certification and Plan of Care (CMS 485), signed by the Physician, is required for all clients receiving skilled services. Skilled services include Nursing, Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy, Speech Therapy, Registered Dietician, and Medical Social Work. 4.2 For skilled cases, the Clinical Manager or RN [Registered Nurse] designee establishes the client's plan of care in conjunction with the Physician and the client/caregiver...Verbal orders are obtained from the Physician to initiate the plan of care which is documented in Locator 23 and signed, and dated by the Clinical Manager, designated RN or therapist. ...4.3 A reassessment is performed at least every (60) days or earlier based on the clients needs ...at which time the plan of care is updated and signed by the Physician. ..."

Reference #2 Facility policy titled, "0-983 Physician's Orders"  states, "...1.0 Immediately after the RN or Therapist (PT, SLP) assesses a client with the need for skilled services, he/she fills out the CMS 485 and sends it to the client's physician for signature. ..."

1. Review of Medical Record #2 on 12/1/21 revealed the following:

a. A Physician Order, dated 11/11/21 and timed 3:56 PM states, "Order Type: Physician Order, Order Description: Move OT [Occupational Therapy] Eval [Evaluation] to next calendar week..."

(i) The line next to "Physician Signature" states, "Do not send."

(ii) There was no evidence that the Physician Order was authenticated.

2. Review of Medical Record #4 on 12/2/21 revealed the following:

a. On the Plan of Care, dated 11/6/21, the section that states, "Attending Physician's Signature and Date Signed" was blank.

b. On 12/2/21 at 11:30 AM, upon interview, Staff #7 stated that the Plan of Care was sent to the Physician on 11/12/21 and expected to be signed by 11/26/21.

c. There was no evidence that the Plan of Care was authenticated.

3. Review of Medical Record #11 on 12/1/21 revealed the following:

a. The Plan of Care indicated that Patient #11's SOC (Start Of Care) was initiated on 9/20/21. Patient #11 received the following services: Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy and Skilled Nursing.

(i) The Plan of Care was not signed and dated by the Physician.

b. A Physician Order, dated 9/22/21 and timed for 9:48 AM, states, "...Verbal Order: Y [Yes] ...Order Type: Add on Discipline" was not signed by a Physician.

(i) The line next to "Physician Signature" states, "Do not send." 

(ii) There was no evidence that the Physician's Order was authenticated.

c. A Physician's Order dated 9/29/21 and timed for 1:25 PM states, "..."Send to Physician: Y [yes] Verbal Order: Y...Order type: Add on Discipline..."

(i) The line next to "Physician Signature" was blank. 

(ii) There was no evidence that the Physician's Order was authenticated.

d. A Physician Order dated 10/5/21 states, "Verbal Order: Y [Yes] ...Order Type: Physician Order Order Description: Increase Metformin to 500 MG [milligrams]...Add Nursing visits weekly x2 [times 2] weeks to monitor blood sugar then D/C [discontinue] when goals..."

(i) The line next to "Physician Signature" states, "Do not send."

(ii) There was no evidence that the Physician Order was authenticated.

4. Staff #14 confirmed the above findings.

source_record.Deficiency Description: Initial Comments - Not A Deficiency Citation
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
This was a Federal Recertification and State Re-licensure survey conducted at Bayada at Inspira, Home Health and Hospice on November 28, 29 & 30, 2023, to determine compliance with 42 CFR Part 484 - Conditions of Participation for Home Health Agencies; and State requirements under Title 8, Chapter 42 - Home Health Agency Licensing Standards.

Standard-level deficiencies were cited.

Infection Prevention
CFR(s): 484.70(a)
Standard: Infection Prevention.  

The HHA must follow accepted standards of practice, including the use of standard precautions, to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observations, staff interviews, and review of facility policy and procedure, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure 1.) hand hygiene is performed before having contact with a patient's intact skin and re-usable equipment; 2.) re-useable equipment is cleaned in accordance with manufacturer's instructions and facility policy, during two of three home visits for Patient 4 (P4) and P5. 

Findings include:

Facility policy titled, "Hand Hygiene" states, "....1.0 Indications for Hand Decontamination. …a. Before and after having and direct client contact with intact skin (bathing, dressing, performing physical examinations, taking a blood pressure or pulse, transferring/lifting, etc.). b. Before applying and after removing gloves... " 

Facility policy titled, "Infection Prevention Procedures for Point of Care Devices" states, "... 3.0 Bayada Issued Tablet or Phone Transported from Home to Home … 3.3 Decontaminate hands when moving from direct client care to tablet. …"

1.) On 11/29/23 at 10:21 AM, during a home visit for P5, Staff 11 (S11), a Physical therapist, was observed applying gloves without first performing hand hygiene. While wearing gloves, S11 proceeded to take the patient's blood pressure, pulse, and temperature and was observed entering information on his/her tablet wearing the same gloves and without decontaminating hands. S11 then brought P5 his/her walker, and followed the patient into the hallway and into the Wellness Center, wearing the same gloves, and holding the tablet in one hand. At 10:30 AM, P5 ambulated out of the Wellness Center, and S11 was observed holding the door open with his/her gloved hand. P5 ambulated back to the room with S11, and S11 was then observed removing a paper from a folder in the patient's room, placing the paper near the patient on the counter, touching the patient's walker, and utilizing his/her tablet, while wearing the same gloves. At 10:35 AM, P5 ambulated back to his/her chair and sat down. S11 was observed holding the patient's wrist to check a pulse, still wearing the same gloves, without performing hand hygiene before contact with P5's skin. P5 removed his/her socks and shoes, and S11 physically examined each of the patient's feet, using his/her gloved hand, without first performing hand hygiene.

At 10:41 AM, S11 removed his/her gloves, performed hand hygiene, applied new gloves, and began using his/her tablet. S11 provided P5 the paper from the counter, and then rechecked P5's blood pressure and pulse oximeter, wearing the same gloves, without performing hand hygiene before contact with P5's skin. S11 picked up the tablet, wearing the same gloves. 

2.) Review of the facility policy titled, "Infection Prevention Procedures for Point of Care Devices" states, "... 3.4 Bayada Issued Tablet or Phone Transported from Home to Home … 3.4 "Disinfect tablet or phone using an approved EPA registered disinfectant wipe, and stylus using a 70% isopropyl alcohol wipe or EPA registered disinfectant wipe with gloved hands, at the following time: 3.4.1 Beginning of visit … 3.4.2 Before and after client visit verification signature 3.4.2.1 Client finger - Disinfect tablet screen before and after client touches screen to sign for visit verification with a manufacturer's approved EPA registered disinfectant wipe following the manufacturer's recommended contact time. Note: The manufacturer's approved wipe for the Galaxy device is the PDI brand. …" 

On 11/28/23 at 12:45 PM, during a home visit for P4, S8 (Physical Therapist) was observed using a tablet asking P4 questions. S8 was not observed disinfecting the tablet at the beginning of the visit. At 1:19 PM, S8 was observed placing the tablet on the table in front of P4 without disinfecting the tablet. P4 used his/her finger to sign the tablet. 

On 11/29/23 at 10:21 AM, during a home visit for P5, S11 (Physical Therapist) was observed using a tablet while checking P5's vital signs. S11 was not observed disinfecting the tablet at the beginning of the visit.. At 10:54 AM, S11 was observed disinfecting a tablet with a wipe. source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1): This was a Federal Complaint Survey conducted on July 27, 2021. Bayada at Inspira Home Health and Hospice is not in compliance with the requirements of 42 CFR Part 484, Subpart B requirements for Home Health Agency for this complaint investigation (C# NJ00146875).

Document complaint and resolution
CFR(s): 484.50(e)(1)(ii)
(ii) Document both the existence of the complaint and the resolution of the complaint; and

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on staff interviews, the review of four (4) medical records, review of facility policies, procedures, and documents, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that an investigation was conducted, and findings and resolutions documented, for patient complaints in one (1) out of four (4) patients. 

Findings Include: 

Reference: The facility policy and procedure titled, "11-368 Client Complaints" states, " ... . Our Procedure: 1.0 Definition: A formal complaint is defined as voicing grievances in writing or verbally to Bayada regarding client's treatment or care ... . 3.0 Complaint Process: 3.1 Clients may register complaints orally or in writing to Bayada. ... . 3.3 The Client Services Manager, Clinical Manager, and/or Director investigate and respond to complaints from clients or their representatives promptly and in accordance with applicable state requirements. The client is informed of the findings of the investigation and the decisions rendered to resolve the complaint. 4.0 Documentation: 4.1 All complaints, verbal and written, are documented in the applicable electronic system. This includes the nature of the complaint, the investigation finding, any follow-up action that is needed, and the date of follow-up with the client. Notification to the client is also documented. ... ."

1. On 7/27/21, upon staff interviews regarding patient complaints, the following was indicated:

a. At 11:00 AM, Staff #2 stated that in the event of a patient complaint or grievance, our staff are instructed to reach out to the Manager of the Team of the Office Branch the patient is assigned. The complaint is entered in our electronic system and addressed immediately in real time. 

b. At 2:30 PM, a telephone interview was conducted with Staff #3, in the presence of Staff #1 and Staff #2. Staff #3 stated that Patient #1 had reached out to him/her sometime between 7/16/21 and 7/20/21. Staff #3 verbally shared the notes that were taken during the call and summarized the notes in an email. 

(i) An email written by Staff #3 stated, "This is what I have logged on the call I took, I don't have an exact date, but would have been between 7/16 and 7/20. (Last Name of Patient-Patient #1): PT [Physical Therapy] was great; (Name of Therapist-Staff #5) was wonderful and helpful. (Name of Therapist-Staff #4) came on and was "cooky" and did nothing but create problems; it was dark out when he/she called; took my walker and changed the wheels; seems mad he/she got a call at night." 

c. At 2:50 PM, Staff #3 stated that the verbal complaint/grievance from Patient #1 should have been electronically entered into their complaint system for follow-up and communication to the patient. 

2. The above was confirmed with Staff #1 and Staff #2.

Discharge plans communication
CFR(s): 484.60(c)(3)(ii)
(ii) Any revisions related to plans for the patient's discharge must be communicated to the patient, representative, caregiver, all physicians or allowed practitioner's issuing orders for the HHA plan of care, and the patient's primary care practitioner or other health care professional who will be responsible for providing care and services to the patient after discharge from the HHA  (if any).

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on staff interviews, review of four (4) medical records, and review of facility policy and procedure, it was determined the facility failed to ensure that discharge planning is implemented according to facility policy and procedure for one (1) of four (4) patients.

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy titled, "0-9307 Client Transfer and Discharge-Medicare Certified Home Health and Home Care Offices" states, "... . Our Policy: Appropriate information is exchanged when a client is discharged or transferred. Our Procedure: 3.0 Communication and Documentation Requirements for Discharge and Transfer: ... . 3.1.3 Clients are provided with Discharge Instructions, 0#-2003 upon discharge from (Name of the Facility). ... . A copy of the Discharge Instructions, #0-2003 are kept in the client chart. ... ." 

1. On 7/27/21, upon staff interviews, the following was indicated: 

a. At 12:30 PM, Staff #1 stated that when a patient is discharged from the facility, there are several documents that require patient or care giver signage, such as Notice of Medicare Non-coverage, Home Health Change of Care Notice, and Discharge Instructions.

b. At 12:35 PM, Staff #2 stated that when a patient is discharged from all services at the facility, Discharge Instructions are provided to the patient and/or caregiver. After staff review of instructions with the patient, the patient and/or caregiver will be asked to sign the instructions. A copy of the signed discharge instructions are filed in the medical record. 

2. On 7/27/21, upon review of Medical Record #1, the following was noted:

a. Patient #1 was discharged from the facility on 4/30/21.

(i) There was no copy in the medical record of the patient's signed discharge instructions.

3. Staff #1 and Staff #2 confirmed that there were no discharge instructions in Medical Record #1.

source_record.Deficiency Description: Receive All Services In Plan Of Care
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Receive all services in plan of care
CFR(s): 484.50(c)(5)
Receive all services outlined in the plan of care.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation, medical record review, and staff interview, it was determined the facility failed to assess pulse oximetry, as per a physician's order, on two of four home visits conducted (Patient #1 and Patient #4).  

On 7/29/24 at 12:02 PM, during a home visit with Patient (P) 1, Staff (S) 4, a Registered Nurse, was observed performing an assessment of P1’s vital signs. S4 began the assessment by first obtaining a measurement of P1’s blood pressure, followed by radial pulse, respirations, temperature, and a pain assessment. An assessment of P1’s pulse oximetry was not observed to be performed by S4. 

On 7/30/24 at 10:30 AM, during medical record (MR) review of P1, documentation by S4 for a visit dated 7/29/24, stated, “…Lungs/Breath Sounds [:] … Dyspnea [shortness of breath]: 2 - With moderate exertion (for example, while dressing, using commode or bedpan, walking distances less than 20 feet) [.] Pulse Ox [Oximetry]: [blank] % …” 

The CMS - 485 Form, for certification period from 7/11/2024 to 9/8/2024, states, “… 21. Orders for Discipline and Treatments … [:] … CARE PLAN INTERVENTIONS: … Assess pulse oximeter with admit and prn [as needed] dyspnea – Active 07/11/2024 …”

On 7/30/24 at 12:00 PM, during a home visit with P4, S5, a Physical Therapist, was observed obtaining P4’s vital signs. After obtaining the blood pressure, pulse, and respirations, S5 stated to P4, “what about your breathing?” P4 stated, “what about my breathing? Yeah, I’ve been short of breath.” S5 responded, “do you want a pulse ox [pulse oximetry reading]?” P4 then continued, “...you know, they said I had CHF [Congestive Heart Failure], but then they said I didn’t.” S5 then responded, “what about your pain, are you having any pain right now?” P4 stated, “right now, no.” At 12:10 PM, S5 then began physical therapy exercises with P4 as ordered. An assessment of P4’s pulse oximetry was not observed to be performed by S5.

On 7/31/24 at 10:40 AM, during review of P4's MR, documentation by S5 for a visit dated 7/30/24, stated, “… Vital Signs [:] … PO2 [Pulse Oximetry]: Not Assessed … Dyspnea [:] Dyspnea Severity Scale: 2 …”

The CMS - 485 Form for certification period from 7/11/2024 to 9/8/2024 states, “… 21. Orders for Discipline and Treatments … [:] … CARE PLAN INTERVENTIONS: …  Assess pulse oximeter as orderer [sic] [ordered] AT SOC [Start Of Care] AND IF DYSPNEA OCCURS – Active 06/13/2024 …”

On 7/31/24 at 12:07 PM, during an interview with S1, the Director of Nursing (DON), when asked about the dyspnea numerical scale, indicated on both home health visit observations with P1 and P4, that a numerical scale is utilized for both nursing and physical therapy to assess the level of dyspnea. Nursing uses a scale of 0-4, and a reported score of 2 [two] indicates shortness of breath, “with moderate exertion such as walking distances less than 20 feet.” Whereas physical therapy uses a scale of 0-10. S1 confirmed via a telephone call with S5 (Physical Therapist), that a reported score of 2 [two] indicates “minimal” shortness of breath. S1 confirmed that in both of these instances, a pulse oximetry assessment was not assessed and documented on P1 and P4 as ordered.

N.J.A.C. 8:42-13.2(a)(6)

source_record.Facility Name: Cedar Crest Village, Inc. Home Health Department
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Infection Prevention
CFR(s): 484.70(a)
Standard: Infection Prevention.  

The HHA must follow accepted standards of practice, including the use of standard precautions, to prevent the transmission of infections and communicable diseases.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on observation, document review and staff interview, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that infection guidelines policies are implemented.

Findings include:

Reference #1: Facility policy titled "Bag technique" states, "... Procedure ... 6. ... Hand hygiene will always be completed each time staff is entering the bag ... 10. When the visit is completed, reusable equipment will be cleaned using alcohol, soap and water, or other appropriate solution per manufacturer guidelines."

Reference #2: Facility product "Dispatch Hospital Cleaner Disinfectant Towels with Bleach" states, " ... Applications: Hard, non porous surfaces such as ... patient monitoring equipment ... Direction for Use ... To Clean, Disinfect & Deodorize in One Step: Wipe surface with towel until completely wet. Let stand for one minute."

1. On 4/3/18 during a home visit of Patient #1, Staff #7 was observed entering the bag to retrieve a pre-moistened disposable towel without first sanitizing his/her hands. Staff #7 quickly wiped the blood pressure cuff and placed it back in the bag. Staff #7 failed to let the blood pressure cuff stand completely wet for one minute before placing it back into the bag.

Reference #3: Facility policy titled "Standard Precautions" states, "... 1. Hand hygiene will be performed to prevent cross-contamination between the patient and personnel. ... Before contact with patient... After contact with the patient or objects in the immediate vicinity of the patient... After removal of personal protective equipment (PPE). ... Equipment/Non-disposable Instruments... Reusable medical equipment must be cleaned/disinfected prior to use on another patient and when soiled. ... 2. The HHA will follow the manufacturer's instructions for use and current standards of practice for patient care equipment transport, storage and cleaning/disinfecting. ... ."

1. During a home visit of Patient #2 on 4/3/18, the following was observed:

a. Staff #8 removed a blood pressure cuff and a stethoscope from his/her bag to use for Patient #2.

b. When finished, Staff #8 squirted hand sanitizer in his/her hand and rubbed it on the blood pressure cuff and stethoscope. Staff #8 then placed the blood pressure cuff and the stethoscope back into his/her bag.

c. Upon interview, Staff #8 stated that he/she was unsure why he/she used his/her hand to clean the blood pressure cuff and stethoscope with hand sanitizer.

2. During a home visit of Patient #4 on 4/4/18, the following was observed:

a. Staff #12 prepared to do a dressing change on Patient #4's left leg wound. While wearing clean gloves, Staff #12 picked up a wrapper from the floor and threw it in the trash. He/she then went back to setting up clean supplies for the dressing change.

(i) Staff #12 did not hand sanitize or change gloves after picking up the wrapper from the floor.

b. Staff #12 donned gloves and removed Patient #4's wound dressing.

(i) He/she did not hand sanitize prior to donning gloves.

3. Staff #1 and Staff #4 confirmed the above findings.

source_record.Facility Name: Cedar Crest Village, Inc. Home Health Department
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Infection control
CFR(s): 484.70(b)(1)(2)
Standard: Control.  

The HHA must maintain a coordinated agency-wide program for the surveillance, identification, prevention, control, and investigation of infectious and communicable diseases that is an integral part of the HHA's quality assessment and performance improvement (QAPI) program. The infection control program must include:



(1) A method for identifying infectious and communicable disease problems; and



(2) A plan for the appropriate actions that are expected to result in improvement and disease prevention.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on review of facility documents and staff interviews, it was determined that the facility failed to include a plan for appropriate actions that are expected to result in improvement after identifying problems with infection control.

Findings include:

1. On 4/3/18, the Health Committee meeting minutes for the third quarter of 2017 were reviewed. The meeting minutes indicated that there were two (2) urinary tract infections with Foley catheters, two (2) wound infections, one (1) conjunctivitis, and one (1) infection of unknown origin. 

a. The Health Committee meeting minutes state, "No trends identified. There will be continued to monitoring [sic] urinary tract infections with Foley, wounds and other infections."

2. On 4/3/18, the Infection Control Committee meeting minutes for the fourth quarter of 2017 were reviewed. The meeting minutes indicated that there were ten (10) urinary tract infections for the fourth quarter, four (4) of which were with a urinary device. There were three (3) wound infections, one (1) ear infection, and one (1) episode of cellulitis.

a. Under the section marked "follow-up," the Infection Control meeting minutes state, "Continue to monitor urinary tract infections and trends."

b. There was no evidence of a plan of action instituted by the facility to address the increase in urinary tract infections and wound infections.

3. Staff #2 and Staff #4 confirmed the above findings.

source_record.Facility Name: Cedar Crest Village, Inc. Home Health Department
source_record.Deficiency Description: Promptly Alert Relevant Physician Of Changes
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Promptly alert relevant physician of changes
CFR(s): 484.60(c)(1)
The HHA must promptly alert the relevant physician(s) to any changes in the patient's condition or needs that suggest that outcomes are not being achieved and/or that the plan of care should be altered.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:

Based on review of 4 medical records and staff interview, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that the physician was notified regarding the change in patient condition, as indicated in the plan of care for Patient #1. 

Finding include:

1. In Medical Record #1, the Home Health Certification And Plan Of Care beginning 3/7/18 stated, " ... Care Plan Interventions: ... Assess weights daily, ... Notify MD [physician] for weight gain of 3 lbs [pounds] in 24 hours or 5 plus pounds in a week."

a. On 3/8/18, a skilled nursing visit was made and the patient weight was recorded as 153.5 lbs. 

(i) On the next nursing visit of 3/15/18, a nurse recorded the following patient weights: "... 3/12/18 - 153 (lbs), 3/13/18 - 156.5 (lbs), 3/14/18 - 156.5 (lbs), 3/15/18 - 155.5 (lbs). 

(ii) There was no evidence in the visit note of 3/15/18 that the physician had been notified by the patient of the 3 pound weight increase in 24 hours. There was no evidence that the physician was notified by the nurse of the patient's weight increase.

(iii) On 3/16/18, an unscheduled nursing visit was made for a medication spill and indicated the patient had a scheduled physician appointment. At that time, the physician was notified of the patient's weight gain.

2. The above was confirmed by Staff #4.

source_record.Facility Name: Cedar Crest Village, Inc. Home Health Department
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Interdisciplinary assessment of the patient
CFR(s): 484.75(b)(1)
Ongoing interdisciplinary assessment of the patient;

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
 

Based on review of 4 medical records and staff interview, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that an issue identified by a member of the interdisciplinary team was assessed for Patient #1.

Findings include:

1. Patient #1 began receiving Home Health Services beginning 3/7/18. 

a. Upon review of the medical record, a Physical Therapy Revisit Note, dated 3/13/18, indicated that the patient had right 5th digit toe pain and had a podiatrist appointment on 3/19/18. Care coordination was done with the nursing staff regarding the "5th right toe symptoms."

b. A Skilled Nurse Visit Note, dated 3/15/18, failed to indicate an assessment of the right 5th digit toe, but it indicated that the patient had a podiatrist visit on 3/19/18.

c. On 3/19/18 and subsequent visits (3), there was no evidence by the nursing staff that addressed the outcome of the podiatrist visit related to the 5th digit toe.

d. On 3/20/18, Physical Therapy addressed the outcome from the podiatrist visit.

2. The above was confirmed by Staff #4.

source_record.Facility Name: Cedar Crest Village, Inc. Home Health Department
source_record.Statement of Deficiency Text (Part 1):
Interventions and patient response
CFR(s): 484.110(a)(2)
All interventions, including medication administration, treatments, and services, and responses to those interventions;

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on medical record review and staff interviews, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure that documentation in the medical record included patient responses to interventions.

Findings include:

a. On the Physical Therapy Evaluation form dated 3/9/18, the pre-treatment and post-treatment vital signs were not documented.

3. Review of Medical Record #4 on 4/4/18 revealed the following:

a. On the Physical Therapy Evaluation form dated 3/19/18, the patient's pre-treatment temperature and post-treatment vital signs were not documented.

4. Staff #1 and Staff #4 confirmed the above findings.

Health, psychosocial, functional, cognition
CFR(s): 484.55(c)(1)
The patient's current health, psychosocial, functional, and cognitive status;

This Element is not met as evidenced by:
Based on one (1) of three (3) home visits (#7), staff interviews and review of policy and procedure, it was determined that the facility failed to ensure implementation of their policy and procedure for Pain Assessment.  

Findings include:

Reference: Facility policy titled, "Pain Assessment, Management and Education" states, "... Policy: ...When pain is identified, a more comprehensive pain assessment will be completed. .... Procedure: ... 2. When .... the clinician identifies pain, the following in-depth pain assessment information should be obtained whenever possible:  A. Pain intensity using a rating scale .... . Pain intensity notation should include a patients initial intensity level of pain and the pain intensity level after medication regime or pain relief modalities. ... .

1. On 10/6/2021 during a routine home visit with Patient #7 by Staff #6, a nurse, the following was revealed:

a. At 11:30 AM, Staff #6 conducted an assessment of Patient #7's right foot for his/her cellulitis and swelling of the area. Staff #6 touched the top of the patient's foot and asked the patient, "On a scale of 1 - 10, what is your pain rating?" The patient answered, "there's more pain when you touch it." Staff #7 then asked for a number and the patient stated, "10." Staff #6 then proceeded to measure the area.

2. At 11:55 AM, after leaving the patient's home, upon interview, Staff #6 confirmed he/she did not ask the patient to provide a pain level when the foot is not touched. 

3. The above findings were confirmed by Staff #2 on 10/7/2021 at 12:15 PM.

This Element is not met as evidenced by:

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on staff interviews and a review of facility documents, it was determined the facility failed to ensure participation in a full-scale exercise that was community-based or individual, facility-based functional exercise; or documentation of an actual natural or man-made emergency that required activation of the emergency plan.

Findings include:

Facility policy titled, “Emergency Preparedness Plan”, dated 06/2021, stated, “…Response: … 10. Exercise scenarios will allow the agency to evaluate its handling of communication, resources and assets, staff and patients. Each exercise whether test or actual, will be documented and evaluated for effectiveness… Review of the emergency management drill will consist of the following: 1. Reassess status of continued operations. 2. Check status of staff and patients. 3. Make any repairs or adjustments needed to continue operations… 4. An annual evaluation of the agency’s hazard vulnerability analysis and EPP including its objectives, scope, vulnerability, and effectiveness will be conducted…”

Facility document titled, “Emergency Preparedness Plan”, dated 03/2023, stated, “… IX) Post Disaster Recovery: After-Action Assessment and After-Action Report (ARR): After resolution of the emergency the HSS will evaluate the effectiveness of the Emergency Management Plan, including the Communication Plan, through the completion of an After-Action Assessment and Report (AAR)… The AAR is designed as a retrospective analysis of the HSS’s response to the emergency to identify the strength’s and areas of improvement… Retention of After-Action Report: The After-Action Report will be kept by the organization for a period of three (3) years after the date of the emergency…”

On 05/21/26, a review of the facility’s Emergency Preparedness Plan (EPP) documentation was conducted. The EPP documentation lacked evidence of participation in a full-scale exercise that was community-based or an individual, facility-based functional exercise; or documentation of an actual natural or man-made emergency that required activation of the emergency plan.

On 05/21/26 at 10:55 AM, an interview was conducted with Staff (S)1. S1 stated, the facility did not have any documentation of an actual emergency that occurred during the past two years. S1 stated, “We certainly lived through snow storms this winter, but did not document the response.” When questioned about the last full-scale exercise conducted at the facility, S1 provided surveyors with facility document titled, “Post-Power Shutdown Action Plan."

A review of facility document titled “Post-Power Shutdown Action Plan” was conducted. The document provided the plan, purpose, and objectives for a community-based exercise to be conducted on 06/05/25. The document lacked evidence that the exercise had been conducted and EPP procedures were evaluated for effectiveness.

On 05/22/26 at 11:33 AM, an interview was conducted with S1. S1 confirmed the facility was unable to provide evidence that the “Post-Power Shutdown Action Plan” exercise had been conducted and EPP procedures were evaluated for effectiveness. S1 was unable to provide surveyors with any additional documentation of full-scale exercises or actual emergencies conducted during the past two years.

Encoding and transmitting OASIS
CFR(s): 484.45(a)
Standard: An HHA must encode and electronically transmit each completed OASIS assessment to the CMS system, regarding each beneficiary with respect to which information is required to be transmitted (as determined by the Secretary), within 30 days of completing the assessment of the beneficiary.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on review of agency pre-survey report and staff interview, it was determined the facility failed to ensure timely transmission of Outcome and Assessment Information Set (OASIS) assessments within 30 days of completion of beneficiary assessments.

Findings include:

A review of the iQIES HHA (Home Health Agency) Error Summary by Agency report, with a reporting period of 01/01/25 to 12/31/25, revealed 57 (8.51%) assessments submitted to iQIES greater than 30 days after completion of the beneficiary assessments. The findings were confirmed with Staff (S) 1 on 05/22/26 at 11:33 AM.

At 11:33 AM, an interview was conducted with S1. S1 explained that the facility works with an offsite coder and a clinical reimbursement nurse (CRN) to complete the OASIS documents and submit them to iQIES. S1 further explained that he/she and the CRN meet weekly to discuss any delays. S1 was unsure of the facility’s benchmark goal, he/she said, “its likely 5%.” S1 stated that they are aware of the delays but were waiting for first quarter data results before creating an improvement plan.

Performance improvement projects
CFR(s): 484.65(d)(1)(2)
Standard: Performance improvement projects. 

 Beginning July 13, 2018 HHAs must conduct performance improvement projects. 



(1) The number and scope of distinct improvement projects conducted annually must reflect the scope, complexity, and past performance of the HHA's services and operations.  



(2) The HHA must document the quality improvement projects undertaken, the reasons for conducting these projects, and the measurable progress achieved on these projects.

This Standard is not met as evidenced by:
Based on staff interview and review of facility documents, it was determined the facility failed to ensure a performance improvement project was conducted annually.

Findings include:

On 05/21/26, a review of the facility’s Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) documentation from 2025 and 2026 was conducted. The QAPI documentation lacked evidence that a performance improvement project was conducted in 2025 or 2026.

On 05/21/26 at 11:50 AM, an interview was conducted with Staff (S)1. S1 confirmed the facility was unable to provide evidence that a performance improvement project was conducted annually. S1 stated, projects are discussed in QAPI meetings and they should be documented, however he/she was unable to locate the documentation.
